entries.ipa: /əˈlɔŋ wɪð/ (also /əˈlɑŋ/ with the cot–caught merger; with also /wɪθ/)
entries.meaning: Joins a second party or a second item to what has already been named, either as company on the way or as one more thing in the pile. It is the everyday additive of American speech and writing, equally at home in a shipping manifest and in conversation.
examples: She rode out to the site along with two state inspectors.
The dog came along with us on every trip that summer.
The sale includes the appliances along with all the patio furniture.
Bring a photo ID along with a copy of the lease.
The governor, along with three of her aides, was subpoenaed.
Interest, along with late fees, is added to the balance every month.

senses.head: In the company of
body: Two people or things moving or acting together.
examples: She rode out to the site along with two state inspectors.
The dog came along with us on every trip that summer.

senses.head: In addition to
body: One more item added to a list, a price, or a transaction.
examples: The sale includes the appliances along with all the patio furniture.
Bring a photo ID along with a copy of the lease.

senses.head: Appended to a subject
body: The verb still agrees with the original subject alone.
examples: The governor, along with three of her aides, was subpoenaed.
Interest, along with late fees, is added to the balance every month.

entries.русский: вместе с, наряду с — присоединяет спутника или ещё один пункт; число глагола не меняет
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, or gerund — never a finite clause, never a bare or to-infinitive
entries.pattern: [clause] along with [noun phrase] · [subject], along with [noun phrase], [singular verb] · Along with [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.contrast: Interchangeable with together with, which is the more written of the two. Neither can do the instrumental work of plain with — you cut bread with a knife, not along with one. And along with is a preposition, not and: it does not make a singular subject plural.
entries.see also: together with, as well as, in addition to, coupled with, complete with, in collaboration with, in the company of, with

entries.meaning: Adds a second item while keeping the first one in the foreground. This asymmetry is the whole point of the word: A and B gives the two equal billing, A as well as B makes B the afterthought — which is exactly why the verb never notices it.
examples: The clinic treats adults as well as children.
She speaks Portuguese as well as Spanish.
He runs the front desk as well as handling the schedule.
The grant covers tuition as well as paying for books.
She wanted to direct as well as act.
The mayor, as well as two council members, was invited.
Fuel, as well as labor, accounts for most of the increase.

senses.head: In addition to a noun
examples: The clinic treats adults as well as children.
She speaks Portuguese as well as Spanish.

senses.head: Linking two verbs
body: The second verb goes to -ing, unless a modal or a to-infinitive already governs it.
examples: He runs the front desk as well as handling the schedule.
The grant covers tuition as well as paying for books.
She wanted to direct as well as act.

senses.head: Appended to a subject
body: Singular subject, singular verb.
examples: The mayor, as well as two council members, was invited.
Fuel, as well as labor, accounts for most of the increase.

entries.pronunciation note: both instances of as reduce, and the weak form is what you actually hear · uhz-WEL-uhz
entries.русский: а также, равно как и — добавляет второй пункт вторым планом; глагол согласуется с первым
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, or gerund; a bare infinitive when the main verb is itself a bare or to-infinitive (She can act as well as sing) — never a that-clause
entries.pattern: [clause] as well as [noun phrase] · [subject], as well as [noun phrase], [singular verb] · [verb-ing] … as well as [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: As well as is not and. And builds a compound subject and takes a plural verb; as well as subordinates the second item, so the verb agrees with the first subject alone — The pitcher, as well as two relievers, was ejected. Keep it apart from the comparative adverbial as well as meaning "as skillfully as" (He plays as well as she does), which is a different construction with a clause after it.
entries.see also: along with, together with, in addition to, besides, plus, not to mention

entries.meaning: Presents a thing along with everything that outfits it. It sells hard, and because it sells so hard, half its working life is spent being sarcastic.
examples: The cabin rents complete with linens, firewood, and a canoe.
They delivered the grill complete with a cover and a full tank of propane.
He showed up in a three-piece suit, complete with pocket watch.
The lobby has been restored complete with the original brass mailboxes.
We got the whole presentation, complete with the slideshow.
It was a classic family dinner, complete with an argument about the will.

senses.head: Listing what comes with a thing
examples: The cabin rents complete with linens, firewood, and a canoe.
They delivered the grill complete with a cover and a full tank of propane.

senses.head: In descriptions of costume, staging, and setting
examples: He showed up in a three-piece suit, complete with pocket watch.
The lobby has been restored complete with the original brass mailboxes.

senses.head: Sarcastically, for an unwelcome extra
examples: We got the whole presentation, complete with the slideshow.
It was a classic family dinner, complete with an argument about the will.

entries.русский: в комплекте с — вещь идёт со всем оснащением; часто иронично о нежеланном довеске
entries.register: neutral; a fixture of advertising, real-estate copy, and description
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun — no gerund, no finite clause, no infinitive
entries.pattern: [noun] complete with [noun phrase] · [clause], complete with [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Complete with is not including. Including names a member of a set that has already been counted; complete with presents the extra as equipment the whole thing arrives furnished with. It is also positionally restricted where including is not: it postmodifies a noun or trails a clause and cannot open a sentence — ✗ Complete with a canoe, the cabin rents by the week. Against together with, which merely adds, complete with implies the addition finishes the picture, and that implication is what makes it the standard vehicle for a dry joke.
entries.see also: including, together with, along with, coupled with, with

entries.meaning: Joins two factors and reports what they do together. Reporters and analysts reach for it whenever one cause alone would be too simple an explanation.
examples: Low inventory, coupled with cheap credit, pushed prices past any honest appraisal.
Coupled with the new tariffs, the shipping delays wiped out the quarter.
The grant carries a five-year commitment coupled with an annual audit.
A guilty plea coupled with full restitution usually keeps a first offender out of prison.
Coupled with having to retrain the whole staff, the software change cost them a season.
The rent increase, coupled with losing two tenants, put the building underwater.
Fatigue, coupled with poor visibility, was listed as the probable cause.
The deductible, coupled with the monthly premium, makes the policy a bad deal.

senses.head: Naming two factors behind one result
examples: Low inventory, coupled with cheap credit, pushed prices past any honest appraisal.
Coupled with the new tariffs, the shipping delays wiped out the quarter.

senses.head: Adding a condition to an obligation or an offer
examples: The grant carries a five-year commitment coupled with an annual audit.
A guilty plea coupled with full restitution usually keeps a first offender out of prison.

senses.head: With a gerund
examples: Coupled with having to retrain the whole staff, the software change cost them a season.
The rent increase, coupled with losing two tenants, put the building underwater.

senses.head: Appended to a subject
body: The verb agrees with the original subject alone.
examples: Fatigue, coupled with poor visibility, was listed as the probable cause.
The deductible, coupled with the monthly premium, makes the policy a bad deal.

entries.русский: в сочетании с, вкупе с — два фактора действуют совместно и дают названный результат
entries.register: neutral to formal; the analyst's and the reporter's word
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, or gerund — never a finite clause
entries.pattern: [noun phrase], coupled with [noun phrase], [verb agreeing with the first noun] · Coupled with [noun phrase], [clause] · coupled with [verb-ing]
entries.variants: combined with, paired with, allied to — the same construction under different metaphors
entries.contrast: Where along with and together with merely add a second item, coupled with claims the two work on each other to produce the result the main clause names. It is the causal member of the additive family, and swapping it for and loses that claim. Its agreement behavior is the family rule: Drought, coupled with two failed harvests, was enough to empty the valley — singular, because coupled with is a preposition and not a conjunction.
entries.see also: along with, together with, in addition to, complete with, plus

entries.meaning: Names something extra that stands alongside what the main clause says, with no suggestion that either item is the more important. Because it is transparently compositional, it survives in formal writing where plus and besides would sound casual.
examples: In addition to the fine, he lost his license for ninety days.
The apartment comes with a parking space in addition to a storage locker.
In addition to working full time, she takes two night classes.
In addition to running the shop, he does all the bookkeeping himself.
The principal, in addition to four teachers, was placed on leave.
In addition to the tuition, students pay a lab fee and a parking permit.

senses.head: Adding a noun
examples: In addition to the fine, he lost his license for ninety days.
The apartment comes with a parking space in addition to a storage locker.

senses.head: Adding an activity — always -ing
examples: In addition to working full time, she takes two night classes.
In addition to running the shop, he does all the bookkeeping himself.

senses.head: Appended to a subject
body: The verb agrees with the subject alone.
examples: The principal, in addition to four teachers, was placed on leave.
In addition to the tuition, students pay a lab fee and a parking permit.

entries.русский: в дополнение к, помимо — to здесь предлог, поэтому дальше герундий, а не инфинитив
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, or gerund — the to here is a preposition, so a bare infinitive is an error: in addition to working, never in addition to work full time. No finite clause.
entries.pattern: In addition to [noun phrase], [clause] · [clause] in addition to [noun phrase] · in addition to [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: The to-trap it shares with look forward to, object to, and be used to: the to is a preposition and demands -ing. Against as well as, it is heavier and more likely to open a sentence; against besides, it is unambiguous — besides can also mean "except for", and in addition to never can.
entries.see also: as well as, along with, besides, plus, over and above, not to mention

entries.meaning: Names the partner a piece of work was done with, and says something about what kind of partnership it was. American writing reaches for these wherever a bare with would be ambiguous between "accompanied by", "by means of", and "jointly with" — a byline, a grant credit, and a press release cannot afford that ambiguity.
examples: The exhibit was mounted in collaboration with the tribal historic preservation office.
She wrote the score in collaboration with her brother.
In collaboration with researchers at Michigan, the lab published three papers in a year.
The clinic operates in cooperation with the county health department.
The festival is presented in cooperation with the National Park Service.
Local police executed the warrant in concert with federal agents.
The two funds bought the shares in concert with one another and had to file as a group.
Wages have risen in tandem with rents, so nobody is any better off.
The rollout will proceed in tandem with retraining the entire dispatch staff.
The museum, in collaboration with two universities, is digitizing the collection.
The state, in cooperation with four counties, was named in the consent decree.

senses.head: Joint work, with a named partner
body: The core use of in collaboration with.
examples: The exhibit was mounted in collaboration with the tribal historic preservation office.
She wrote the score in collaboration with her brother.
In collaboration with researchers at Michigan, the lab published three papers in a year.

senses.head: Institutional sponsorship or consent
body: Where in cooperation with is the fixed form.
examples: The clinic operates in cooperation with the county health department.
The festival is presented in cooperation with the National Park Service.

senses.head: Coordinated and simultaneous action
body: Where in concert with is the fixed form, including in its adversarial legal sense.
examples: Local police executed the warrant in concert with federal agents.
The two funds bought the shares in concert with one another and had to file as a group.

senses.head: Two things moving as a linked pair
body: Where in tandem with is the fixed form, and the only one of the four that readily takes a gerund.
examples: Wages have risen in tandem with rents, so nobody is any better off.
The rollout will proceed in tandem with retraining the entire dispatch staff.

senses.head: Appended to a subject
body: The verb agrees with the original subject alone.
examples: The museum, in collaboration with two universities, is digitizing the collection.
The state, in cooperation with four counties, was named in the consent decree.

entries.русский: в сотрудничестве с, совместно с — называет партнёра по совместной работе
entries.register: neutral to formal; institutional — bylines, credit lines, press releases, grant reports
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun, normally a named party — a person, an agency, a company, a university. No finite clause, no infinitive, and for three of the four no gerund: ✗ in collaboration with rebuilding the archive. In tandem with is the exception and takes a gerund freely (in tandem with rebuilding the archive), because what it pairs is two processes rather than two parties.
entries.pattern: [clause] in collaboration with [named party] · In collaboration with [named party], [clause] · [subject], in collaboration with [party], [singular verb]
entries.variants: in cooperation with /ɪn koʊˌɑpəˈreɪʃən wɪð/, in-koh-op-uh-RAY-shun with — the institutional side of the same relation, and the standard wording on a government or nonprofit credit line; in concert with /ɪn ˈkɑnsərt wɪð/, in-KON-surt with — coordinated and simultaneous, the choice when the point is timing; in tandem with /ɪn ˈtændəm wɪð/, in-TAN-dum with — two things working as a linked pair, and the only one of the four that takes a process as comfortably as a person. In partnership with and in conjunction with belong to the same family.
entries.contrast: All four are periphrastic with, and plain with would carry the bare meaning in every sentence below; what the longer forms buy is a claim about how the two parties are joined. In collaboration with claims joint creative or professional work — the partner actually contributed. In cooperation with claims institutional consent and assistance, which is why it appears on permits and credit lines and why it can be literally true when the partner did almost nothing. In concert with claims simultaneity and coordination, and it is the one that survives in adversarial contexts: acting in concert with is a term of art in American securities law for parties whose holdings are counted as one block. In tandem with claims a linked pair, and takes an abstract process where the others want a partner. Against in conjunction with, the colorless "together with" of this group, which makes no claim at all about who did what. Like everything else in this file they are prepositions and not conjunctions, so the verb keeps agreeing with the original subject.
entries.see also: together with, along with, coupled with, in the company of, in addition to, with

entries.respell: weak /ɪn ðə ˈkʌmpəni əv/, reduced /ɪn ðə ˈkʌmpəniə/
entries.meaning: Places a person among other people and lets that fact color the sentence. It is what English reaches for when the point is not that two people were both present but that one of them was inside the other's orbit.
examples: He was last seen in the company of two men in a gray pickup.
The senator spent the evening in the company of the plaintiffs' lawyers.
She is a different person in the company of her sisters.
In the company of strangers he hardly says a word.
Six months in the company of people who read put a dent in his television habit.
He spent that whole summer in the company of a crowd his mother could not stand.
The painting hangs in the company of three Vermeers.
The novel belongs in the company of the best work of that decade.
He behaves much better in company.
The two frigates sailed in company as far as the Azores.

senses.head: Reporting whom somebody was with
body: Common in police, court, and news writing.
examples: He was last seen in the company of two men in a gray pickup.
The senator spent the evening in the company of the plaintiffs' lawyers.

senses.head: Describing the effect of the company kept
examples: She is a different person in the company of her sisters.
In the company of strangers he hardly says a word.

senses.head: In praise or in judgment — the evaluative use
examples: Six months in the company of people who read put a dent in his television habit.
He spent that whole summer in the company of a crowd his mother could not stand.

senses.head: Figuratively, of a thing set among its peers
body: A learned extension, and the one place the object need not be alive.
examples: The painting hangs in the company of three Vermeers.
The novel belongs in the company of the best work of that decade.

senses.head: Not a preposition — bare in company
body: Nothing follows it, no one is named, and it is an adverb meaning "among other people".
examples: He behaves much better in company.
The two frigates sailed in company as far as the Azores.

entries.русский: в обществе кого-л., в компании кого-л. — только о людях: среди кого человек находился
entries.register: formal to neutral; literary, biographical, and legal
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun naming people — no gerund, no finite clause, and normally no inanimate object: in the company of strangers, not ✗ in the company of a suitcase. The determiner is frozen: never ✗ in a company of, never ✗ in company of.
entries.pattern: [clause] in the company of [person or people] · In the company of [person or people], [clause] · last seen in the company of [person]
entries.variants: in company with — dated, and chiefly nautical or commercial (sailed in company with the Ariel). Bare in company, with nothing after it, is an adverb and not this preposition at all (he behaves better in company): it names no one, and the object is the whole test.
entries.contrast: A periphrasis of accompanying with, and the only member of the accompaniment family restricted to human company. Where along with and together with add a second item to a list, in the company of describes the situation of the subject — it says whom he was among, and it very often carries a judgment about whether that was good for him. Against among, which is neutral about the relationship and takes a group rather than a set of named people; against accompanied by, which points at a subordinate escort where in the company of points at the surrounding party. Its natural homes are the police blotter, the biography, and any sentence about one person's influence on another.
entries.see also: along with, together with, in collaboration with, without, with

entries.meaning: Picks out one or more members of a set that has just been named, or folds a component into a total. It does not claim the list that follows is complete, and in careful writing it should not be used as if it were: if the set really is exhausted, write namely or consisting of.
examples: Nine passengers, including the pilot, walked away from the crash.
Several states, including Ohio and Nevada, have already certified.
Everyone including me had to retake the certification.
The rate is $180 a night, including breakfast.
That comes to $42 including tax and delivery.
All benefits, including but not limited to health and dental coverage, continue through June.
The tenant pays all utilities, including without limitation gas, electric, water, and trash.
The audit covers everything, including how the reserve fund was spent.
Several questions remain, including whether the lease can be broken at all.
The job has its costs, including driving ninety minutes each way.
She listed her objections, including having to sign a five-year lease.

senses.head: Naming members of a set
body: A pronoun after it goes in the objective case — including me, never including I.
examples: Nine passengers, including the pilot, walked away from the crash.
Several states, including Ohio and Nevada, have already certified.
Everyone including me had to retake the certification.

senses.head: Counting something into a total
examples: The rate is $180 a night, including breakfast.
That comes to $42 including tax and delivery.

senses.head: The drafting formula
body: Used when the list must be read as open-ended.
examples: All benefits, including but not limited to health and dental coverage, continue through June.
The tenant pays all utilities, including without limitation gas, electric, water, and trash.

senses.head: Before a wh-clause
body: The complement is a question folded into a noun slot.
examples: The audit covers everything, including how the reserve fund was spent.
Several questions remain, including whether the lease can be broken at all.

senses.head: With a gerund
examples: The job has its costs, including driving ninety minutes each way.
She listed her objections, including having to sign a five-year lease.

entries.русский: включая, в том числе — называет отдельных членов множества; список не считается полным
entries.type: marginal/participial (fully grammaticalized — it needs no subject to control it)
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, gerund, or a wh-clause (including how the money was spent, including whether the lease can be broken) — one of the very few prepositions in this file that takes one. Never a that-clause and never a tensed clause on its own: ✗ including it was raining.
entries.pattern: [total set], including [member], … · [amount] including [component] · including but not limited to [list]
entries.contrast: The mirror of excluding. Against inclusive of, which is a commercial and contractual word attaching to a noun, including attaches loosely to a whole clause and is unrestricted in register. Against postposed included (tax included), which follows its noun rather than preceding it. Note that including names a sample, not the whole list — which is why American drafters write including without limitation when they need to say so out loud.
entries.see also: including without limitation, inclusive of, excluding, exclusive of, not counting, plus

entries.meaning: Opens a list and says out loud that the list is only a sample. It is the most common belt-and-suspenders phrase in American contract drafting, and outside a contract it is almost always four words too many.
examples: Tenant shall pay all utilities, including without limitation gas, electric, water, and trash removal.
The release covers all claims, including without limitation claims for wrongful termination.
Contractor is responsible for all permits, including but not limited to electrical and plumbing permits.
The policy excludes intentional acts, including but not limited to arson and fraud.
Licensee may not modify the software, including, without limitation, by decompiling, disassembling, or reverse engineering it.
The estate passes all personal property, including, without limitation, furniture, vehicles, and the contents of any safe deposit box.
The grant covers travel, including without limitation airfare and lodging. (edit to including)
She asked about the fees, including but not limited to the origination charge. (edit to including)

senses.head: In contracts, opening a non-exhaustive list
examples: Tenant shall pay all utilities, including without limitation gas, electric, water, and trash removal.
The release covers all claims, including without limitation claims for wrongful termination.

senses.head: The commoner American variant
examples: Contractor is responsible for all permits, including but not limited to electrical and plumbing permits.
The policy excludes intentional acts, including but not limited to arson and fraud.

senses.head: Set off by commas, where the list runs long
examples: Licensee may not modify the software, including, without limitation, by decompiling, disassembling, or reverse engineering it.
The estate passes all personal property, including, without limitation, furniture, vehicles, and the contents of any safe deposit box.

senses.head: Outside a contract — where it should be cut
body: The tag buys nothing in ordinary prose, and editors delete it on sight.
examples: The grant covers travel, including without limitation airfare and lodging. (edit to including)
She asked about the fees, including but not limited to the origination charge. (edit to including)

entries.русский: включая, но не ограничиваясь — юр. формула, открывающая заведомо неполный перечень
entries.register: formal; American legal drafting almost exclusively
entries.type: complex (a frozen drafting formula built on including)
entries.complement: whatever bare including takes — noun phrase, list of noun phrases, objective-case pronoun, or gerund — because without limitation is a parenthetical tag on including and not a preposition of its own. Never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [total set], including without limitation [list] · [total set], including but not limited to [list] · [total set], including, without limitation, [list]
entries.variants: including but not limited to — the same formula, and by a wide margin the commoner of the two in American contracts; including without limiting the generality of the foregoing is the long-winded third form, now mostly confined to older boilerplate. British drafting prefers including without limitation; American drafting splits between the first two.
entries.contrast: Bare including already names a sample rather than the whole list, so in ordinary prose the tag adds nothing and an editor will cut it. It survives because courts do not reliably read including that way: under the interpretive canon ejusdem generis — Latin, "of the same kind", and something an American meets only in a brief or an opinion — a following list can be read as narrowing the general word that introduced it, and drafters add without limitation to shut that reading down. Against inclusive of, which declares what a stated price already contains rather than opening a list; against to the exclusion of, which is not about lists at all. Note the punctuation split: American drafters write including without limitation unpunctuated in a short list and including, without limitation, inside commas when the list runs long.
entries.see also: including, inclusive of, excluding, exclusive of, to the exclusion of, not counting

entries.respell: weak /ɪnˈklusɪv əv/, reduced /ɪnˈklusɪvə/ before a consonant
entries.meaning: Declares what a stated price, figure, or period already contains. It exists because contracts and invoices need a word that cannot be misread, and it buys that precision at the cost of sounding like a contract.
examples: All quoted prices are inclusive of shipping and handling.
Rent is $2,150 a month, inclusive of water, sewer, and trash.
The flat fee is inclusive of all filing costs.
Salaries are stated inclusive of the employer's retirement contribution.
The package is inclusive of airfare, transfers, and two guided excursions.
Headcount stands at 240, inclusive of contractors and seasonal staff.
The blackout period runs March 3 to March 9, inclusive of both dates.
Coverage is inclusive of the first and the last day of the term.

senses.head: Of a price, a rate, or a fee
body: The commonest use by far.
examples: All quoted prices are inclusive of shipping and handling.
Rent is $2,150 a month, inclusive of water, sewer, and trash.
The flat fee is inclusive of all filing costs.

senses.head: Of a figure, a headcount, or a package
examples: Salaries are stated inclusive of the employer's retirement contribution.
The package is inclusive of airfare, transfers, and two guided excursions.
Headcount stands at 240, inclusive of contractors and seasonal staff.

senses.head: Of a span of dates
body: Where American English usually says through instead.
examples: The blackout period runs March 3 to March 9, inclusive of both dates.
Coverage is inclusive of the first and the last day of the term.

entries.русский: офиц. включая, с учётом — что уже входит в названную цену или величину
entries.register: formal; chiefly commercial, contractual, and hospitality writing
entries.complement: noun phrase only — no gerund, no clause
entries.pattern: [noun] inclusive of [noun phrase] · [price] is inclusive of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The exact opposite of exclusive of, and the stiff twin of including. Including can float anywhere in a sentence; inclusive of almost always postmodifies a noun or follows the verb be. Do not confuse the preposition with the adjective inclusive in a date range (March 3 through March 9 inclusive), which takes no of — and which American English rarely needs, since through is already inclusive where British to is not.
entries.see also: including, exclusive of, excluding, plus

entries.meaning: Adds a second item only to say that it lies even further beyond whatever was just denied. It is a scaling device rather than a true addition: the first item marks the floor and let alone points past it.
examples: There wasn't enough money for repairs, let alone a new roof.
He doesn't have a driver's license, let alone a car.
She can't walk to the mailbox, let alone run a 10K.
Most of them couldn't find the building, let alone get past the front desk.
The road isn't paved, let alone plowed.
Nobody goes down there in daylight, let alone after dark.
Who has time for lunch, let alone a two-hour meeting?
The team barely made the playoffs, let alone a deep run.

senses.head: After a negative, before a noun phrase
examples: There wasn't enough money for repairs, let alone a new roof.
He doesn't have a driver's license, let alone a car.

senses.head: Before a bare infinitive matched to the verb before it
examples: She can't walk to the mailbox, let alone run a 10K.
Most of them couldn't find the building, let alone get past the front desk.

senses.head: Before an adjective, an adverb, or a prepositional phrase
examples: The road isn't paved, let alone plowed.
Nobody goes down there in daylight, let alone after dark.

senses.head: In questions and after near-negatives
examples: Who has time for lunch, let alone a two-hour meeting?
The team barely made the playoffs, let alone a deep run.

entries.pronunciation note: the t flaps between vowels · let-uh-LOHN
entries.русский: не то что, не говоря уже о — только после отрицания: то, что тем более невозможно
entries.type: marginal (a frozen imperative that has become a connective)
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, adjective, adverb, prepositional phrase, gerund, or a bare infinitive matched to the verb before it (can't walk, let alone run) — never a finite clause, and never a to-infinitive when the verb before it is bare: ✗ can't walk, let alone to run.
entries.requires: a negative, near-negative, or question earlier in the sentence — not, never, nobody, nothing, hardly, barely, too … to, can't. Without one it is ungrammatical: ✗ He can drive, let alone fly a plane.
entries.pattern: [negative clause], let alone [phrase parallel to what preceded] · can't [bare verb], let alone [bare verb] · not [noun], let alone [noun]
entries.variants: much less — fully interchangeable in American English; never mind (informal) and still less (formal) do the same work.
entries.contrast: Let alone is the mirror image of not to mention and to say nothing of. All three add a second item at the end, but not to mention upgrades — what follows is the heavier item actually in play — while let alone downgrades: what follows is the more extreme thing that is even further out of reach. He can't drive, let alone fly a plane says flying is the harder claim; reverse the two and the sentence collapses. Note also that whatever follows must be parallel to what preceded it: a bare verb answers a bare verb, a noun answers a noun.
entries.see also: not to mention, to say nothing of, besides, in addition to, short of

entries.meaning: Adds one last item under the pretense of skipping it. The pretense is the whole device: what follows lands harder than what came before precisely because the speaker claimed not to be bringing it up.
examples: The repair took three weeks and two thousand dollars, not to mention a rental car.
She runs the department and teaches two seminars, not to mention a research group of nine.
The apartment is tiny, not to mention four flights up.
The plan is expensive, not to mention flatly illegal.
He had to redo three years of taxes, not to mention explaining the whole thing to his brother.
Moving in February means ice and a truck deposit, not to mention taking a week off work.
The lease is a bad deal, not to mention the fact that the building is for sale.
He missed three deadlines, not to mention the fact that nobody could reach him for a week.

senses.head: Adding a heavier item at the end of a list
examples: The repair took three weeks and two thousand dollars, not to mention a rental car.
She runs the department and teaches two seminars, not to mention a research group of nine.

senses.head: Adding an adjective
body: A construction almost no other preposition allows.
examples: The apartment is tiny, not to mention four flights up.
The plan is expensive, not to mention flatly illegal.

senses.head: With a gerund
examples: He had to redo three years of taxes, not to mention explaining the whole thing to his brother.
Moving in February means ice and a truck deposit, not to mention taking a week off work.

senses.head: With the fact that, where a clause is unavoidable
examples: The lease is a bad deal, not to mention the fact that the building is for sale.
He missed three deadlines, not to mention the fact that nobody could reach him for a week.

entries.pronunciation note: the t of not glottalizes and to is always the weak /tə/, never /tu/ · naht-tuh-MEN-shun
entries.русский: не говоря уже о — добавляет более весомый пункт под видом умолчания; только в конце фразы
entries.type: marginal (a frozen infinitival that has become a preposition)
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, gerund, adjective, or a wh-clause. A that-clause only through the fact that (not to mention the fact that nobody asked). Never a bare finite clause.
entries.pattern: [clause], not to mention [noun phrase] · [adjective], not to mention [adjective] · [clause], not to mention [verb-ing]
entries.variants: to say nothing of — a shade more formal and fully interchangeable. Distinguish let alone, which reverses the polarity: it needs a negative before it and downgrades what follows (He can't drive, let alone fly a plane), where not to mention upgrades.
entries.contrast: Against in addition to and as well as, which are neutral, not to mention is rhetorical: it pretends to omit the item while naming it, so whatever follows is always the heavier or the more damning of the two. It is also positionally fixed — it comes at the end of what it adds to and never opens a sentence: ✗ Not to mention the cost, the plan is impractical; write The plan is impractical, not to mention ruinously expensive.
entries.see also: to say nothing of, let alone, in addition to, as well as, besides, over and above, plus

entries.respell: weak /ɑn ˈtɑp əv/, reduced /ɑnˈtɑpə/ before a consonant
entries.meaning: Piles one more demand onto a load that was already heavy. It is the American complaint word of the additive family, and the only one that presupposes the addition is unwelcome.
examples: On top of the rent, they pay their own utilities and trash.
The clinic charges a facility fee on top of the doctor's bill.
On top of working two jobs, she's finishing a degree at night.
On top of having to repaint, we found rot under the siding.
On top of everything else, the furnace quit on the coldest night of the year.
She lost the contract and, on top of that, the client wants the deposit back.
On top of what the movers charged, we paid two weeks of storage.
On top of whatever the insurer covers, there's a $2,000 deductible.

senses.head: In addition to — with the second item as a burden
examples: On top of the rent, they pay their own utilities and trash.
The clinic charges a facility fee on top of the doctor's bill.

senses.head: With a gerund
examples: On top of working two jobs, she's finishing a degree at night.
On top of having to repaint, we found rot under the siding.

senses.head: The fixed phrase on top of everything else
examples: On top of everything else, the furnace quit on the coldest night of the year.
She lost the contract and, on top of that, the client wants the deposit back.

senses.head: Before a wh-clause
examples: On top of what the movers charged, we paid two weeks of storage.
On top of whatever the insurer covers, there's a $2,000 deductible.

entries.pronunciation note: the of loses its /v/ exactly as it does in out of · on-TOP-uv
entries.русский: вдобавок к, сверх — разг., с оттенком жалобы: ещё одна тягота поверх прежних
entries.register: neutral; the additive sense is conversational and nearly always aggrieved
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, or gerund (on top of paying rent); a nominal wh-clause is possible in the additive sense (on top of what the movers charged). Never a that-clause and never a to-infinitive: ✗ on top of pay rent. Bare on top is an adverb and takes no object — the berries go on top — and that is the test: the preposition must have something after it.
entries.pattern: On top of [noun phrase], [clause] · [clause] on top of [noun phrase] · on top of [verb-ing] · on top of everything else
entries.contrast: The literal sense — the keys are on top of the refrigerator — is a spatial preposition and is covered with the complex prepositions; what belongs in this file is the additive one. Against in addition to, which is neutral and formal, on top of is informal and carries a complaint built in: the second item is a burden piled on the first, which is why on top of the rent is idiomatic and on top of the bonus sounds odd. Against besides, it can never be read as "except for". A third idiom, on top of meaning "in full control of" (she's on top of every deadline), is a separate sense again.
entries.see also: in addition to, as well as, besides, over and above, plus, not to mention

entries.meaning: Names what is added once an obligation has already been discharged. It is the standard phrase for a bonus, an overage, and a duty gone beyond.
examples: The bonus is paid over and above base salary.
Any expenses over and above the retainer must be approved in writing.
She did that work over and above anything the job actually required.
The district demands sixty hours of training over and above the state minimum.
Over and above the cost, there's the question of whether anyone would use it.
The building is unsafe, and over and above that, it isn't even zoned for offices.

senses.head: Money added to an amount already owed
examples: The bonus is paid over and above base salary.
Any expenses over and above the retainer must be approved in writing.

senses.head: Effort or service beyond a required minimum
examples: She did that work over and above anything the job actually required.
The district demands sixty hours of training over and above the state minimum.

senses.head: Adding a further consideration to an argument
examples: Over and above the cost, there's the question of whether anyone would use it.
The building is unsafe, and over and above that, it isn't even zoned for offices.

entries.pronunciation note: the and is always reduced to /ən/ or /n̩/ · OH-vur-un-uh-BUV
entries.русский: сверх, помимо — прибавка поверх уже выполненного обязательства или нормы
entries.register: formal to neutral; standard in compensation, contracts, and budgets
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun; a gerund is possible but uncommon (over and above having to repay the advance). Never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [amount] over and above [amount] · [clause] over and above [noun phrase] · Over and above [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.contrast: Over and above is in addition to with one extra claim built in: the addition sits on top of a baseline that has already been satisfied. A bonus over and above base salary means the salary was already paid in full; an hour over and above the minimum means the minimum was already met. Where in addition to is neutral about the first item, over and above certifies it. Do not read the phrase compositionally — it is frozen, and neither over nor above keeps its spatial meaning inside it.
entries.see also: in addition to, as well as, plus, not to mention, besides

entries.meaning: Adds one quantity or item to another. It began life as the Latin word for "more" in arithmetic and spread outward from there into prices, packages, and finally into casual speech as a discourse connector.
examples: Six plus four is ten.
The perimeter is the length plus the width, doubled.
Rent is $1,400 a month plus utilities.
At closing you'll owe the principal plus accrued interest.
He brought his cousin plus two friends nobody had met.
She got the promotion plus a corner office.
It's too far to drive. Plus, the parking is impossible.
The seats are terrible, and plus they cost twice as much.

senses.head: Arithmetic addition
examples: Six plus four is ten.
The perimeter is the length plus the width, doubled.

senses.head: With the addition of
body: A cost, a component, an extra.
examples: Rent is $1,400 a month plus utilities.
At closing you'll owe the principal plus accrued interest.

senses.head: And also
body: An extra item, slightly informal.
examples: He brought his cousin plus two friends nobody had met.
She got the promotion plus a corner office.

senses.head: As a sentence adverb — not a preposition
body: No object follows; informal.
examples: It's too far to drive. Plus, the parking is impossible.
The seats are terrible, and plus they cost twice as much.

entries.русский: плюс — прибавляет число или пункт; предлог, поэтому глагол остаётся в единственном числе
entries.register: neutral as a preposition; the sentence-initial Plus, is informal
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun; a gerund is possible but rare (plus having to repaint). Never a finite clause. The word is also an adjective (a plus sign, an A plus), a noun (that's a real plus), and an informal sentence adverb (Plus, it's cheaper) — in those uses it has no object and is not a preposition.
entries.pattern: [number] plus [number] · [amount] plus [noun phrase] · Plus, [clause] (adverb — informal)
entries.contrast: Plus is not and. And makes a compound subject and takes a plural verb; plus is a preposition, so The base salary plus the bonus was more than he expected keeps the singular. In arithmetic, Two plus two is four is the standard form. Against minus, its arithmetic opposite; against in addition to, its formal equivalent — a job application should not begin a sentence with Plus.
entries.see also: minus, give or take, in addition to, on top of, over and above, as well as, including, not to mention

entries.meaning: Names one more item while claiming to pass over it. Like not to mention, the pretense is the whole device, and register is the only thing that separates the two.
examples: The delay cost them the season, to say nothing of the money.
Two of the exhibits were mislabeled, to say nothing of the one that never arrived.
He'd have to sell the house, to say nothing of explaining it to his sister.
Rewriting the code took a month, to say nothing of testing it.
The proposal is expensive, to say nothing of legally doubtful.
The trip was long and cold, to say nothing of pointless.
The deal is bad on its face, to say nothing of the fact that nobody on the board has read it.
She was unqualified, to say nothing of the fact that she had been fired twice.

senses.head: Adding a heavier item at the end of a list
examples: The delay cost them the season, to say nothing of the money.
Two of the exhibits were mislabeled, to say nothing of the one that never arrived.

senses.head: With a gerund
examples: He'd have to sell the house, to say nothing of explaining it to his sister.
Rewriting the code took a month, to say nothing of testing it.

senses.head: Adding an adjective or a further judgment
examples: The proposal is expensive, to say nothing of legally doubtful.
The trip was long and cold, to say nothing of pointless.

senses.head: With the fact that, where a clause is unavoidable
examples: The deal is bad on its face, to say nothing of the fact that nobody on the board has read it.
She was unqualified, to say nothing of the fact that she had been fired twice.

entries.pronunciation note: weak /tə ˈseɪ ˈnʌθɪŋ əv/, reduced /tə ˈseɪ ˈnʌθɪŋə/ before a consonant — the to is always the weak /tə/, never /tu/ · tuh-SAY-NUTH-ing-uv
entries.русский: не говоря уже о — книжн. двойник not to mention: добавляет более веский довод
entries.type: complex (a frozen infinitival that has become a preposition)
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, gerund, or adjective; a that-clause only through the fact that. Never a bare finite clause, and — because the of is a preposition — never a bare infinitive: to say nothing of paying for it, not ✗ to say nothing of pay for it.
entries.pattern: [clause], to say nothing of [noun phrase] · [clause], to say nothing of [verb-ing] · [adjective], to say nothing of [adjective]
entries.variants: not to mention — the spoken equivalent, and interchangeable in almost every context
entries.contrast: The formal twin of not to mention; the difference is register, not sense. To say nothing of is what you meet in edited prose, not to mention is what you hear. Both are rhetorical rather than neutral — whatever follows is the heavier item, named under the pretense of being skipped — and both are positionally fixed at the end of what they add to: ✗ To say nothing of the cost, the plan is impractical. Against let alone, which reverses the polarity and downgrades what follows, to say nothing of always upgrades.
entries.see also: not to mention, let alone, in addition to, besides, over and above, as well as

entries.meaning: Attaches a second item to the first in writing that wants to sound deliberate. It is the standard formula in deeds and contracts, where together with all appurtenances has been boilerplate for centuries, and it carries a trace of that formality into ordinary prose.
examples: The deed conveys the parcel together with all easements and rights of way.
Please return the signed form together with a check for the filing fee.
Heat, together with the humidity, makes the afternoons unbearable.
Send the transcript together with three letters of recommendation.
The chairman, together with two board members, was named in the suit.
The principal, together with any unpaid interest, becomes due on demand.

senses.head: Accompanying an item in a transaction or a submission
examples: The deed conveys the parcel together with all easements and rights of way.
Please return the signed form together with a check for the filing fee.

senses.head: Adding one factor to another
examples: Heat, together with the humidity, makes the afternoons unbearable.
Send the transcript together with three letters of recommendation.

senses.head: Appended to a subject
body: Singular verb.
examples: The chairman, together with two board members, was named in the suit.
The principal, together with any unpaid interest, becomes due on demand.

entries.русский: вместе с, совместно с — офиц. вариант along with; на число глагола не влияет
entries.register: formal to neutral; standard in legal and conveyancing language
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, or gerund — never a finite clause
entries.pattern: [clause] together with [noun phrase] · [subject], together with [noun phrase], [singular verb]
entries.contrast: The formal twin of along with, and the two are freely interchangeable in meaning. Neither is instrumental — that is plain with. Like every word in this section, it is a preposition and does not pluralize a singular subject.
entries.see also: along with, as well as, in addition to, coupled with, complete with, in collaboration with, in the company of, with

entries.meaning: Sets an item outside the claim being made — either by exempting it from a generalization or, in the additive reading, by putting it beside one. The literal reading, "at a distance from", is still live and is the source of both.
examples: Apart from a scratch on the bumper, the car is in perfect shape.
Everyone apart from the two interns had already gone home.
Apart from being the cheapest option, it's also the fastest.
Apart from the tuition, there are lab fees and a parking permit.
Apart from what the neighbors told us, we know nothing about the family.
Apart from whether the roof will hold, there's the wiring to think about.
He stood apart from the rest of the group, saying nothing.
Keep the recyclables apart from the regular trash.

senses.head: Except for
body: Subtracting a qualification.
examples: Apart from a scratch on the bumper, the car is in perfect shape.
Everyone apart from the two interns had already gone home.

senses.head: In addition to
body: Adding one more item, usually signaled by also or a negative.
examples: Apart from being the cheapest option, it's also the fastest.
Apart from the tuition, there are lab fees and a parking permit.

senses.head: Before a wh-clause
examples: Apart from what the neighbors told us, we know nothing about the family.
Apart from whether the roof will hold, there's the wiring to think about.

senses.head: Separate from
body: The literal spatial sense, and the source of the other three.
examples: He stood apart from the rest of the group, saying nothing.
Keep the recyclables apart from the regular trash.

entries.русский: кроме, если не считать — но при отрицании или с also, наоборот, «помимо, вдобавок к»
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, gerund, or a wh-clause (apart from what the neighbors told us, apart from whether it's legal) — never a that-clause and never a tensed clause on its own
entries.pattern: Apart from [noun phrase], [clause] · [clause] apart from [noun phrase] · apart from [verb-ing] · apart from [wh-clause]
entries.contrast: Apart from and aside from mean the same thing; aside from is the more American of the two and apart from the more British, though both are current in the United States. Both are ambiguous between "except for" and "in addition to", and only context settles it: after a plain positive claim they subtract, but before also, too, or as well, or alongside a negative, they add.
entries.see also: aside from, besides, except for, other than, outside of

entries.meaning: The default American way to fence off an exception before making a general claim. It opens sentences more comfortably than almost anything else in this file, which is why it turns up constantly in reviews, summaries, and complaints.
examples: Aside from a few typos, the draft is ready to send.
Nobody aside from the two of us knows the combination.
Aside from running the shop, he coaches a Little League team.
Aside from being illegal, it's a terrible idea.
Aside from whether it's legal, it's a terrible way to treat people.
Aside from what the inspector wrote down, nobody has said a word to us.
Aside from the cost, there's the question of whether it will even fit.
Aside from one bad winter, we've never had trouble with the pipes.

senses.head: Except for
examples: Aside from a few typos, the draft is ready to send.
Nobody aside from the two of us knows the combination.

senses.head: In addition to
examples: Aside from running the shop, he coaches a Little League team.
Aside from being illegal, it's a terrible idea.

senses.head: Before a wh-clause
examples: Aside from whether it's legal, it's a terrible way to treat people.
Aside from what the inspector wrote down, nobody has said a word to us.

senses.head: Opening a concession before the main point
examples: Aside from the cost, there's the question of whether it will even fit.
Aside from one bad winter, we've never had trouble with the pipes.

entries.русский: кроме, если не считать; также «помимо, вдобавок к» — амер. вариант apart from
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, gerund, or a wh-clause (aside from what it costs, aside from whether it's legal) — never a that-clause and never a tensed clause on its own
entries.pattern: Aside from [noun phrase], [clause] · [clause] aside from [noun phrase] · aside from [verb-ing] · aside from [wh-clause]
entries.contrast: Identical in meaning to apart from; the difference is geography, not sense. American writers reach for aside from first, British writers for apart from. Like apart from, it swings between subtraction and addition on the polarity of the sentence around it. Against except for, it is looser — except for commits to subtraction, aside from does not.
entries.see also: apart from, besides, except for, other than, outside of

entries.meaning: Built on the verb bar exactly as barring is, and now nearly frozen. In its one thriving American use it does no grammatical work beyond intensifying a superlative that has already been made.
examples: It's the best barbecue in the state, bar none.
She is the finest trial lawyer in this building, bar none.
Every seat was sold, bar a handful in the last row.
All the runners finished bar one, who pulled up at mile eighteen.
Bar a late collapse, they'll take the division. (an American would write barring)
The court barred him from the property for a year. (verb)
They met at a bar two blocks from the courthouse. (noun)

senses.head: The fixed American phrase
body: After a superlative: with no exceptions.
examples: It's the best barbecue in the state, bar none.
She is the finest trial lawyer in this building, bar none.

senses.head: General exception — chiefly British
body: An American ear hears this as an import.
examples: Every seat was sold, bar a handful in the last row.
All the runners finished bar one, who pulled up at mile eighteen.
Bar a late collapse, they'll take the division. (an American would write barring)

senses.head: Not a preposition — the verb and the noun
body: The preposition takes an object and means "except"; the verb means "to shut out" and takes a direct object of its own, and the nouns are unrelated to both.
examples: The court barred him from the property for a year. (verb)
They met at a bar two blocks from the courthouse. (noun)

entries.русский: кроме, за исключением — в амер. англ. живо лишь в обороте bar none «без исключений»
entries.register: formal and chiefly British in free use; standard in American English only inside the fixed phrase bar none
entries.complement: noun phrase — no gerund, no clause
entries.pattern: [superlative claim], bar none · all bar [number] (chiefly British) · bar [noun phrase] (chiefly British)
entries.contrast: In American English bar survives almost entirely in bar none, a fixed tag meaning "with no exceptions at all" that follows a superlative. Where a British writer uses bar freely, an American writes barring or except for. Do not confuse the preposition with the verb bar (barred from the premises) or the several nouns.
entries.see also: barring, except for, save, but

entries.meaning: Fences off the one thing that could go wrong and then makes the prediction anyway. It is the single most useful hedge in American reporting, because it lets a writer commit to a forecast while naming its escape hatch.
examples: Barring a late snowstorm, the roads should be clear by Friday.
Barring injuries, this is the deepest roster they've had in years.
Barring something unforeseen, closing is set for the fifteenth.
Every member voted yes, barring two who abstained.
The archive is complete, barring a handful of volumes lost in the fire.
Barring getting called in, I'm free all weekend.
Barring the river coming up again, the crews will be finished by Thursday.

senses.head: Excluding a contingency from a prediction
examples: Barring a late snowstorm, the roads should be clear by Friday.
Barring injuries, this is the deepest roster they've had in years.
Barring something unforeseen, closing is set for the fifteenth.

senses.head: Plain exception
body: Slightly formal, less common than sense 1.
examples: Every member voted yes, barring two who abstained.
The archive is complete, barring a handful of volumes lost in the fire.

senses.head: With a gerund, and with an object plus a gerund
examples: Barring getting called in, I'm free all weekend.
Barring the river coming up again, the crews will be finished by Thursday.

entries.русский: если не будет, за исключением — оговорка к прогнозу: называет возможную помеху
entries.register: neutral; a staple of forecasting and sports and business journalism
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund — never a finite clause. Not barring it rains; write barring rain or switch to the conjunction unless.
entries.pattern: Barring [noun phrase], [clause] · [clause] barring [noun phrase] · barring [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: Barring names a future contingency that would spoil an otherwise confident prediction; except for subtracts a real member from a set that already exists. Barring an injury looks forward, except for the injury looks back. Against failing, which is its near mirror: barring X frames X as the unwelcome disruption, failing X frames X as the outcome you were hoping for.
entries.see also: bar, failing, short of, except for, absent

entries.meaning: Sets a small deduction aside before endorsing the whole. It is included here for readers of older books, not as a word to use.
examples: Bating a few small errors of transcription, the manuscript is faithful to the original.
The account is complete, bating the two pages torn from the ledger.
The terms were agreed, bating the question of the boundary line.
Bating his temper, he was as fine a foreman as the yard ever had.
All the company came away satisfied, bating one gentleman who had lost his hat.

senses.head: Setting a small deduction aside from a record or an agreement
examples: Bating a few small errors of transcription, the manuscript is faithful to the original.
The account is complete, bating the two pages torn from the ledger.
The terms were agreed, bating the question of the boundary line.

senses.head: Excepting one person or one trait from a judgment
examples: Bating his temper, he was as fine a foreman as the yard ever had.
All the company came away satisfied, bating one gentleman who had lost his hat.

entries.русский: устар. за исключением, не считая — встречается только в книгах XVIII–XIX вв.
entries.complement: noun phrase — never a clause
entries.pattern: Bating [noun phrase], [clause] · [clause], bating [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: An archaic cousin of excepting and saving, formed from the verb abate, "to take away". No living American writes it; you meet it only in eighteenth- and nineteenth-century prose, where it means "leaving out of account". Modern equivalents: excepting, apart from, leaving aside. Do not confuse it with baiting (luring), and note that the bated of with bated breath is the same root but a frozen idiom, not this preposition.
entries.see also: excepting, saving, save, excluding

entries.meaning: Puts one more item next to what has been said, or — after a negative — carves one out. It is the oldest of the additive prepositions and the only one that has also become a discourse marker, which is now what most Americans use it for.
examples: Besides the mortgage, they're carrying two car loans.
Who else is coming besides your brother?
No one besides the surgeon was allowed in the room.
There's nothing in the refrigerator besides condiments.
Besides teaching, she edits a quarterly journal.
Besides costing twice as much, the new system is slower.
It's too far, and besides, I don't have the money.
I'm not going. Besides, I wasn't invited.

senses.head: In addition to
examples: Besides the mortgage, they're carrying two car loans.
Who else is coming besides your brother?

senses.head: Except for
body: Nearly always after a negative or an all-inclusive word.
examples: No one besides the surgeon was allowed in the room.
There's nothing in the refrigerator besides condiments.

senses.head: With a gerund
examples: Besides teaching, she edits a quarterly journal.
Besides costing twice as much, the new system is slower.

senses.head: As an adverb — not a preposition
body: No object; means "anyway" or "moreover".
examples: It's too far, and besides, I don't have the money.
I'm not going. Besides, I wasn't invited.

entries.русский: кроме, помимо — «вдобавок к», а после отрицания «за исключением»; ср. beside «рядом с»
entries.register: neutral; the adverb use is conversational
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, or gerund — never a finite clause. A what-phrase after it (besides what he told us) is a fused relative, which is a noun phrase and not a clause; the test is that a plain noun can replace it (besides his statement). As an adverb it takes no object at all (Besides, it's too late), and that is its commonest use in speech.
entries.pattern: Besides [noun phrase], [clause] · [negative or question] besides [noun phrase] · besides [verb-ing] · Besides, [clause] (adverb)
entries.contrast: Beside vs. besides. Beside without the -s means "at the side of" and belongs with the position prepositions, along with the two frozen idioms beside the point and beside himself. Besides with the -s means "in addition to" or "except for", and is also an adverb meaning "anyway". Sit beside me / Nobody besides me came. Writing besides the point, or beside the salary there's a bonus, is a real and frequent error. Against except for and in addition to, besides is the ambiguous one — careful writers pick the unambiguous word when the reading matters.
entries.see also: apart from, aside from, in addition to, not to mention, other than, except for

entries.meaning: Subtracts one member from a set that has already been declared total. Because it depends entirely on that earlier totalizing word, it feels less like a preposition and more like a second half of a construction — which is why it also lives inside a handful of frozen quantifying phrases.
examples: Everyone but Marcus signed the petition.
The store is open every day but Sunday.
Nobody but you would have noticed.
He'd go anywhere but back to that office.
Any weekend but this one would work.
There was nothing to do but wait for the tow truck.
There is nothing left to say but congratulations.
They had no choice but to postpone the wedding.
With the bridge closed there was no option but to double back.
The season was nothing but injuries and rain delays.
The bill is all but dead in committee.
One cannot but admire the nerve of it. (formal)
I called twice, but nobody picked up. (conjunction — two clauses, no object)
The paint is dry but still tacky in one corner. (conjunction — two adjectives)
The tank was but half full when they set out. (adverb, "only" — formal and dated)

senses.head: Except, after a universal or a negative
examples: Everyone but Marcus signed the petition.
The store is open every day but Sunday.
Nobody but you would have noticed.

senses.head: Before an adverb or a prepositional phrase
examples: He'd go anywhere but back to that office.
Any weekend but this one would work.

senses.head: Before an infinitive — bare after a do-phrase, to after choice
body: This is the one place learners of English go wrong with but, and the two patterns do not mix.
examples: There was nothing to do but wait for the tow truck.
There is nothing left to say but congratulations.
They had no choice but to postpone the wedding.
With the bridge closed there was no option but to double back.

senses.head: In frozen quantifying phrases
body: Nothing but = only; all but = almost; cannot but = cannot help.
examples: The season was nothing but injuries and rain delays.
The bill is all but dead in committee.
One cannot but admire the nerve of it. (formal)

senses.head: Not a preposition — the conjunction and the adverb
body: The preposition takes an object; the conjunction joins two units of equal rank and takes none, and the adverbial but means "only".
examples: I called twice, but nobody picked up. (conjunction — two clauses, no object)
The paint is dry but still tacky in one corner. (conjunction — two adjectives)
The tank was but half full when they set out. (adverb, "only" — formal and dated)

entries.русский: кроме — только после all, everyone, nothing и т. п.: everyone but me «все, кроме меня»
entries.type: simple; the same form is the coordinating conjunction but (see the conjunctions dictionary) and an adverb in all but
entries.the two infinitives are not interchangea: ✗ nothing to do but to wait, ✗ no choice but resign. Never a finite clause — but that is the conjunction, not this preposition, and but never takes a gerund.
entries.complement: noun phrase or pronoun (objective case in American usage), an adverb or prepositional phrase (anywhere but here, any time but now), a bare infinitive after a do-phrase or after cannot (nothing to do but wait, one cannot but admire it), or a to-infinitive after choice, option, or alternative (no choice but to resign).
entries.requires: an all-inclusive or negative word earlier in the sentence — all, every, everyone, everything, everywhere, no one, nothing, nowhere, any-, a superlative, or a wh- question word. Without one it is ungrammatical: not I saw the movie but the ending, but I saw everything but the ending.
entries.pattern: [universal/negative word] but [noun phrase] · nothing but [noun phrase] · nothing to do but [bare infinitive] · no choice but to [verb] · cannot but [bare infinitive]
entries.contrast: Prepositional but is the tightly restricted twin of except, and where except can stand at the head of a sentence with for, but cannot — there is no ✗ but for the noise in this sense (but for is a separate, counterfactual preposition). Against the conjunction but, which joins two clauses of equal rank and reduces to /bət/: the preposition takes an object and is usually stressed.
entries.case note: American usage takes the objective pronoun — everyone but me, no one but him. The traditional rule that a subject-position but-phrase takes the nominative (No one but he knew) is now bookish; No one but him knew is what educated Americans write and say.
entries.see also: except, except for, but for, other than, save

entries.meaning: Names the one thing that stood between the world as it is and the world it would otherwise have been. Its home is American tort law, where but-for causation — the injury would not have occurred but for the defendant's conduct — is the standard test, and it carries that argumentative weight into ordinary prose.
examples: But for your testimony, the case would have been dismissed.
She would have drowned but for the lifeguard on the north jetty.
But for a flat tire, we'd have been there by noon.
But for the pandemic, the restaurant might still be open.
The company would be insolvent but for the parent's guarantee.
But for the officer's failure to secure the scene, the evidence would have been admissible.

senses.head: Naming the decisive cause of a good outcome
examples: But for your testimony, the case would have been dismissed.
She would have drowned but for the lifeguard on the north jetty.

senses.head: Naming the decisive obstacle to one
examples: But for a flat tire, we'd have been there by noon.
But for the pandemic, the restaurant might still be open.

senses.head: In legal and financial argument
examples: The company would be insolvent but for the parent's guarantee.
But for the officer's failure to secure the scene, the evidence would have been admissible.

entries.pronunciation note: weak /ˈbʌt fɚ/ (also written /fər/), and in rapid speech /ˈbʌʔ fɚ/ with a glottal t — BUHT fur
entries.русский: если бы не — юр. и книжн.; главное предложение обязательно с would (have)
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun — never a clause. To take a clause, write but for the fact that.
entries.requires: a counterfactual main clause, with would, would have, might have, or could have.
entries.pattern: But for [noun phrase], [subject] would (have) [verb] · [subject] would (have) [verb] but for [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: But for is not except for. Except for subtracts a real item from a real situation (Except for the dessert, the meal was excellent); but for deletes an item and reports what would have followed (But for the dessert, the meal would have been forgettable). Without says the same thing more plainly, and the everyday American equivalent is if not for, which requires exactly the same counterfactual main clause. It is unrelated to prepositional but.
entries.see also: if not for, without, except for, absent, failing, but

entries.meaning: The plain, unmarked word for taking one member out of a stated whole. Everything else in this section is a stylistic or grammatical variation on it.
examples: Everyone except the two of us went home early.
She remembered nothing except the sound of the brakes.
The museum is open daily except Monday.
The rule applies everywhere except on federal land.
There was nothing to do except apologize and start over.
He had no option except to resign.
I'd have told you except that it wasn't mine to tell.
I'd go, except I'm broke until Friday. (informal)

senses.head: Subtracting a member from a total set
examples: Everyone except the two of us went home early.
She remembered nothing except the sound of the brakes.

senses.head: Before an adverbial — a time, a place, a condition
examples: The museum is open daily except Monday.
The rule applies everywhere except on federal land.

senses.head: Before an infinitive
examples: There was nothing to do except apologize and start over.
He had no option except to resign.

senses.head: Before a clause — with that, or in informal speech without it
body: Here it is a conjunction.
examples: I'd have told you except that it wasn't mine to tell.
I'd go, except I'm broke until Friday. (informal)

entries.русский: кроме, за исключением — требует в предложении all/every/nothing; иначе нужно except for
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, prepositional phrase (except in emergencies), adverb (except here, except yesterday), bare infinitive after do (nothing to do except wait), or to-infinitive (no choice except to agree). A finite clause is possible only through a following conjunction — except that, except when, except if, except where — and at that point except is a conjunction, not this preposition.
entries.requires: an all-inclusive word already in the sentence — all, every, everyone, everything, everywhere, always, nothing, no one, the whole. Without one, use except for.
entries.pattern: [totalizing word] except [noun phrase] · [clause] except [adverbial] · nothing to do except [bare infinitive] · except that [clause] (conjunction)
entries.contrast: Except vs. except for vs. excepting. Use except when a totalizing word is already present (everyone, all, nothing, every day). Use except for when there is no such word, when the phrase opens the sentence, or when the thing subtracted is not the same kind of thing as the set — Except for a few typos, the essay is clean, because typos are not essays. Excepting is formal and now confined to not excepting and always excepting. Sentence-initial bare except — Except the noise, it's fine — is an error. The test for the conjunction is the one used everywhere else in this file: the preposition takes an object, while except that, except when, and except if take a whole finite clause. And do not confuse any of it with the verb accept, which is a different word entirely.
entries.see also: except for, with the exception of, excepting, but, other than, apart from

entries.meaning: Withdraws a qualification from a claim that would otherwise be sweeping. It is the workhorse of the exception family in American English and the safe default when you are unsure whether bare except will hold.
examples: Except for a cracked screen, the phone works fine.
The team played well except for the third quarter.
The house is empty except for a folding chair in the kitchen.
The lot was dark except for one security light over the door.
Except for Tuesdays, my afternoons are open.
Except for having to change planes in Dallas, it was an easy trip.

senses.head: Subtracting a flaw from a general endorsement
examples: Except for a cracked screen, the phone works fine.
The team played well except for the third quarter.

senses.head: Naming the only thing left in an otherwise empty scene
examples: The house is empty except for a folding chair in the kitchen.
The lot was dark except for one security light over the door.

senses.head: Opening a sentence, where bare except cannot
examples: Except for Tuesdays, my afternoons are open.
Except for having to change planes in Dallas, it was an easy trip.

entries.pronunciation note: weak /əkˈsɛpt fɚ/ (also written /fər/), and before a consonant often /əkˈsɛp fɚ/ — ik-SEPT fur
entries.русский: кроме, если не считать — не требует обобщающего слова и может открывать предложение
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, or gerund — never a finite clause
entries.pattern: Except for [noun phrase], [clause] · [clause] except for [noun phrase] · except for [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: Where except needs a totalizing word already in place, except for supplies its own frame and can open a sentence on its own. Except for is also the right choice when the thing subtracted is a different kind of thing from the set — a typo is not an essay, a squeak is not a car. Against but for, which is counterfactual and demands a would-clause; against apart from and aside from, which are looser and may be read additively.
entries.see also: except, with the exception of, but for, apart from, aside from, save for

entries.meaning: Marks an exemption with more ceremony than the situation usually requires. Its two surviving phrases pull in opposite directions: not excepting insists that nothing is exempt, always excepting insists that one thing permanently is.
examples: All employees, not excepting senior partners, must complete the training.
The delegates voted unanimously, not excepting the two who had objected in committee.
The policy covers every kind of loss, always excepting acts of war.
The fee schedule applies to all filings, always excepting emergency petitions.
Every parcel on the block, excepting the corner lot, was rezoned.
All charges were dropped, excepting the count of criminal trespass.

senses.head: Not excepting — including even
examples: All employees, not excepting senior partners, must complete the training.
The delegates voted unanimously, not excepting the two who had objected in committee.

senses.head: Always excepting — with a standing carve-out
examples: The policy covers every kind of loss, always excepting acts of war.
The fee schedule applies to all filings, always excepting emergency petitions.

senses.head: Plain participial exception
body: Dated in American writing.
examples: Every parcel on the block, excepting the corner lot, was rezoned.
All charges were dropped, excepting the count of criminal trespass.

entries.русский: устар./юр. исключая — живо лишь в not excepting «включая даже» и always excepting
entries.complement: noun phrase — no gerund, no clause
entries.pattern: not excepting [noun phrase] · always excepting [noun phrase] · [clause], excepting [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Excepting is what except for replaced. Outside the two fixed emphatics not excepting ("including even") and always excepting ("with the standing exception of"), it sounds stiff or antique in American prose. Excluding is the current neutral participial; saving and bating are the archaic ones.
entries.see also: except, except for, excluding, saving, bating

entries.meaning: Draws a line around a figure or a set and says what is outside it. Because it is neutral and precise, it is the safe word wherever a number has to be defended.
examples: The list price is $34,900, excluding destination charges and tax.
The estimate covers labor only, excluding hauling away the old unit.
Enrollment rose four percent, excluding transfer students.
Revenue grew nine percent excluding currency effects.
Everyone on the roster, excluding the two on injured reserve, made the trip.
The building sleeps twelve, excluding the finished basement.

senses.head: Removing a component from a price
examples: The list price is $34,900, excluding destination charges and tax.
The estimate covers labor only, excluding hauling away the old unit.

senses.head: Removing a group from a statistic
examples: Enrollment rose four percent, excluding transfer students.
Revenue grew nine percent excluding currency effects.

senses.head: Removing a member from a set
examples: Everyone on the roster, excluding the two on injured reserve, made the trip.
The building sleeps twelve, excluding the finished basement.

entries.русский: исключая, не считая — нейтрально-деловое: что не входит в сумму или множество
entries.register: neutral to formal; standard in pricing, statistics, and specifications
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund — never a finite clause
entries.pattern: [total] excluding [noun phrase] · [clause], excluding [noun phrase] · excluding [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: The exact mirror of including, and the modern neutral replacement for excepting. Against except for, it is colder and more quantitative — excluding belongs on an invoice, except for belongs in a sentence. Exclusive of is its formal-contractual variant, not counting its conversational one. Against less and minus, which perform a real arithmetic subtraction: excluding only declares something out of scope.
entries.see also: including, exclusive of, not counting, except for, less, to the exclusion of
