entries.meaning: States what a quoted figure leaves out, in language a court could read. It is the price-list word, and it postmodifies a noun or follows be rather than floating freely through a sentence.
examples: All prices are quoted exclusive of sales tax.
The rent is $1,900 a month, exclusive of utilities.
The retainer is exclusive of court costs and expert witness fees.
The trailer measures forty feet, exclusive of the tongue.
Headcount stands at 212, exclusive of contractors and seasonal staff.
The bid covers materials only, exclusive of the general contractor's fee.
The policy runs from the first of the month, exclusive of the day of purchase.
The notice period is fourteen days, exclusive of weekends and federal holidays.

senses.head: Of a price, a rate, or a fee
examples: All prices are quoted exclusive of sales tax.
The rent is $1,900 a month, exclusive of utilities.
The retainer is exclusive of court costs and expert witness fees.

senses.head: Of a measurement or a headcount
examples: The trailer measures forty feet, exclusive of the tongue.
Headcount stands at 212, exclusive of contractors and seasonal staff.
The bid covers materials only, exclusive of the general contractor's fee.

senses.head: Of a span of dates
examples: The policy runs from the first of the month, exclusive of the day of purchase.
The notice period is fourteen days, exclusive of weekends and federal holidays.

entries.pronunciation note: weak /əkˈsklusɪv əv/, reduced /əkˈsklusɪvə/ before a consonant — ik-SKLOO-siv uv
entries.русский: офиц. не включая, без учёта — что не входит в названную цену или величину
entries.complement: noun phrase only — no gerund, no clause
entries.pattern: [noun] exclusive of [noun phrase] · [price] is exclusive of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The exact opposite of inclusive of, and the contractual twin of excluding. In ordinary American writing, not including or plus tax does the same work without the starch. Do not confuse it with the adjective exclusive meaning "restricted" or "sole" (an exclusive contract), which is a different sense of the same word.
entries.see also: inclusive of, excluding, less, not counting, free of, to the exclusion of

entries.meaning: Names the thing that has to happen, then supplies the plan for when it doesn't. The fixed phrase failing that is by far its commonest form and is the most efficient two words in English for "if that doesn't work".
examples: Failing a settlement, the case goes to trial in October.
Failing agreement between the parties, the matter goes to arbitration.
Ask at the front desk; failing that, call the number posted on the door.
We'll fly out Thursday or, failing that, drive up on Friday.
Failing any objection from the floor, the motion is adopted.
Failing a qualified buyer by June, the bank takes the property.
Payment is due on the first, failing which the account goes to collections.
The tenant must cure the breach within ten days, failing which the lease terminates.

senses.head: Introducing a fallback after a named prerequisite
examples: Failing a settlement, the case goes to trial in October.
Failing agreement between the parties, the matter goes to arbitration.

senses.head: The fixed phrase failing that
examples: Ask at the front desk; failing that, call the number posted on the door.
We'll fly out Thursday or, failing that, drive up on Friday.

senses.head: In procedural and contractual language
examples: Failing any objection from the floor, the motion is adopted.
Failing a qualified buyer by June, the bank takes the property.

senses.head: The formula failing which
body: A fixed relative that hangs a consequence on the failure of what was just required. Formal, and chiefly contractual.
examples: Payment is due on the first, failing which the account goes to collections.
The tenant must cure the breach within ten days, failing which the lease terminates.

entries.русский: за неимением, если не выйдет — вводит запасной вариант: failing that «если не получится»
entries.complement: noun phrase — most often the pronouns that and which (failing that, failing which), and otherwise an abstract noun of outcome (a settlement, agreement, payment). Never a finite clause, never a gerund, never a to-infinitive: ✗ failing to reach a settlement, the case goes to trial is a dangling participle of the verb fail, not this preposition.
entries.pattern: Failing [noun phrase], [clause] · [clause], or failing that, [alternative] · [requirement], failing which [consequence]
entries.contrast: Failing and barring both introduce a condition, and both can often be swapped, but they take opposite attitudes to what they name. Failing X treats X as the outcome you wanted, and what follows is the fallback; barring X treats X as the accident that would spoil an expected result. Absent X is the legal register's version of failing X, and simple without the plain one.
entries.see also: barring, absent, without, short of, but for, if not for

entries.meaning: Puts a tolerance on a number. It is the spoken American way of saying "plus or minus", and its presence is what turns a stated figure into an admitted approximation.
examples: There were sixty people in the room, give or take a dozen.
The lot holds forty cars, give or take a few.
It's about ninety miles from here, give or take five.
The ceiling is nine feet, give or take an inch.
The drive takes two hours, give or take twenty minutes.
They closed on the house in March of '09, give or take a month.
He's been at the paper thirty years, give or take.
The room seats two hundred, give or take.

senses.head: Naming a margin on a count
examples: There were sixty people in the room, give or take a dozen.
The lot holds forty cars, give or take a few.

senses.head: Naming a margin on a measurement or a distance
examples: It's about ninety miles from here, give or take five.
The ceiling is nine feet, give or take an inch.

senses.head: Naming a margin on time
examples: The drive takes two hours, give or take twenty minutes.
They closed on the house in March of '09, give or take a month.

senses.head: With no object — the adverb
body: Nothing follows, and the margin is left vague.
examples: He's been at the paper thirty years, give or take.
The room seats two hundred, give or take.

entries.pronunciation note: the or reduces to /ɚ/ and the three words run together as one · GIV-ur-TAYK
entries.русский: плюс-минус, примерно — допуск в обе стороны от названной величины
entries.type: marginal (a frozen coordination that behaves as a preposition)
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a quantity — a number, a measure, a span of time. No gerund, no clause, and no ordinary object: ✗ give or take the traffic. It can also stand with no object at all (forty people, give or take), and in that use it is an adverb, not a preposition.
entries.pattern: [quantity], give or take [smaller quantity] · [quantity], give or take (adverb — no object)
entries.variants: plus or minus — the technical equivalent, at home on a spec sheet where give or take would sound careless
entries.contrast: Give or take is the only member of this family that subtracts and adds at the same time: it names a margin of error on both sides of a figure, where less and minus deduct in one direction only. Against about and around, which hedge a figure without saying how far the hedge runs, give or take states the tolerance out loud. It attaches only to quantities — a figure with give or take after it is an estimate, never a count.
entries.see also: plus, minus, less, short of, next to

entries.meaning: Deletes one item from the record and reports what would have followed. It is the phrase most Americans reach for when the courtroom but for would sound stiff.
examples: If not for the neighbors, the fire would have taken the whole block.
She'd have missed the flight if not for a delay on the tarmac.
If not for the rain, we'd have finished the roof on Saturday.
If not for one bad quarter, the company would have had a record year.
The bill would have died in committee if not for two senators from farm states.
If not for the second surgery, he'd have been back at work by June.

senses.head: Naming the decisive cause of a good outcome
examples: If not for the neighbors, the fire would have taken the whole block.
She'd have missed the flight if not for a delay on the tarmac.

senses.head: Naming the decisive obstacle
examples: If not for the rain, we'd have finished the roof on Saturday.
If not for one bad quarter, the company would have had a record year.

senses.head: In argument and explanation
examples: The bill would have died in committee if not for two senators from farm states.
If not for the second surgery, he'd have been back at work by June.

entries.pronunciation note: weak /ɪf ˈnɑt fɚ/ (also written /fər/), reduced /ɪf ˈnɑʔ fɚ/ with a glottal t — if-NAHT fur
entries.русский: если бы не — разг. эквивалент but for; главное предложение тоже с would (have)
entries.register: neutral to informal; the everyday American but for
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun — never a gerund and never a finite clause. For a clause, write if it weren't for or if it hadn't been for, which are full clauses with their own subject and verb and not this preposition.
entries.requires: a counterfactual main clause, with would, would have, might have, or could have — exactly what but for requires.
entries.pattern: If not for [noun phrase], [subject] would (have) [verb] · [subject] would (have) [verb] if not for [noun phrase]
entries.variants: if it weren't for, if it hadn't been for, were it not for (formal) — clausal expansions of the same idea, and the route to take when a clause has to follow
entries.contrast: If not for is but for in ordinary clothes: identical in meaning, identical in what it demands of the main clause, and different only in register — but for belongs to legal and formal writing, if not for to speech and general prose. Neither is except for. Except for the dessert, the meal was good reports the world as it is; if not for the dessert, the meal would have been forgettable reports a world that never happened.
entries.see also: but for, without, absent, in the absence of, failing

entries.meaning: Puts one issue to one side so that the argument can get on with the rest. It concedes that the item matters and declines, for the moment, to take it up.
examples: Leaving aside the cost, the schedule alone makes it impossible.
Leaving aside the two outliers, the results are remarkably consistent.
Leaving aside whether the policy is legal, it is certainly unpopular.
Leaving aside what the repairs will run, the car is still worth keeping.
Leaving aside having to move twice, the year went about as well as we hoped.
Leaving aside paying for it, who would even run the program?
The proposal is workable, leaving aside the question of who pays for it.
Enrollment held steady all year, leaving aside a dip in the spring semester.

senses.head: Postponing an issue before making a point
examples: Leaving aside the cost, the schedule alone makes it impossible.
Leaving aside the two outliers, the results are remarkably consistent.

senses.head: Before a wh-clause
examples: Leaving aside whether the policy is legal, it is certainly unpopular.
Leaving aside what the repairs will run, the car is still worth keeping.

senses.head: With a gerund
examples: Leaving aside having to move twice, the year went about as well as we hoped.
Leaving aside paying for it, who would even run the program?

senses.head: Trailing a clause
examples: The proposal is workable, leaving aside the question of who pays for it.
Enrollment held steady all year, leaving aside a dip in the spring semester.

entries.русский: оставляя в стороне, если отвлечься от — вопрос не отрицается, а откладывается
entries.register: neutral to formal; a staple of argument and analysis
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, gerund, or a wh-clause (leaving aside whether it's legal, leaving aside what it costs) — never a that-clause and never a tensed clause on its own
entries.pattern: Leaving aside [noun phrase], [clause] · [clause], leaving aside [noun phrase] · leaving aside [wh-clause] · leaving aside [verb-ing]
entries.variants: setting aside, putting aside, leaving out, leaving to one side (more formal) — freely interchangeable
entries.contrast: Where excluding takes an item out of a count and except for takes it out of a claim, leaving aside takes it out of the discussion: the item is not denied, only postponed, which is what lets it govern a wh-clause where most of this family cannot. Against apart from and aside from, which can be read additively, leaving aside is unambiguously subtractive. It is a true preposition here and not a dangling participle — nobody in the main clause has to be doing the leaving.
entries.see also: excluding, apart from, aside from, except for, not counting, excepting

entries.respell: weak /ləs/ when it sits unstressed between two figures
entries.meaning: Subtracts one figure from another in the language of statements and settlements. It is the only word in this file that is genuinely restricted to money and measurable quantities.
examples: The settlement was $80,000, less attorney's fees.
She cleared the invoice amount less a two percent early-payment discount.
You'll get the deposit back less any charges for damage.
Net pay is gross salary less withholding and benefit contributions.
Revenue less cost of goods sold gives you gross profit.
Book value is original cost less accumulated depreciation.
The lease runs for one year less a day.
The parcel is a full acre less the strip taken for the easement.
The estate distributes the remaining balance less administrative expenses.
There is less traffic on the bridge after nine. (quantifier — no object)
The second bid came in less expensive by about a third. (comparative adverb)

senses.head: Deducting a charge from a sum
examples: The settlement was $80,000, less attorney's fees.
She cleared the invoice amount less a two percent early-payment discount.
You'll get the deposit back less any charges for damage.

senses.head: In the standing formulas of accounting
body: The deduction is a named line item and the whole phrase is a definition.
examples: Net pay is gross salary less withholding and benefit contributions.
Revenue less cost of goods sold gives you gross profit.
Book value is original cost less accumulated depreciation.

senses.head: Deducting a period or a measure
body: Chiefly legal and surveying language.
examples: The lease runs for one year less a day.
The parcel is a full acre less the strip taken for the easement.
The estate distributes the remaining balance less administrative expenses.

senses.head: Not a preposition — the quantifier and the comparative adverb
body: Here less modifies a noun or an adjective directly and has no object of its own; the preposition always has one.
examples: There is less traffic on the bridge after nine. (quantifier — no object)
The second bid came in less expensive by about a third. (comparative adverb)

entries.русский: за вычетом, минус — бухг. и юр.: вычет из суммы (less tax «за вычетом налога»)
entries.complement: noun phrase naming an amount or a deduction — no gerund, no clause, no personal object (less him is not English)
entries.pattern: [amount] less [deduction] · [amount] less any [deduction]
entries.contrast: Less and minus both subtract, but less is the accountant's word and takes an abstract deduction (less tax, less depreciation, less attorney's fees), while minus is the arithmetic and everyday word (ten minus three, showed up minus his coat). Less is never casual and never means "without". Keep the preposition apart from the quantifier less of the fewer/less dispute (less traffic, less expensive) — that less modifies a noun or an adjective directly and has no object of its own.
entries.see also: minus, excluding, exclusive of, plus, give or take, short of

entries.meaning: Takes one quantity away from another, and by extension takes a thing away from a person who ought to have it. The arithmetic sense is the oldest; the everyday "lacking" sense is a twentieth-century American extension and still carries a joking edge.
examples: Nine minus four is five.
Take the total minus whatever you've already paid.
It was minus twelve at the airport this morning.
The forecast has us at minus five by Sunday night.
Your share is the sale price minus closing costs.
The refund is the ticket price minus a $35 service fee.
He came back from the trip minus a suitcase and a phone.
She showed up to the interview minus a résumé.
She got an A minus on the final. (adjective)
The commute is the one real minus of the job. (noun)

senses.head: Arithmetic subtraction
examples: Nine minus four is five.
Take the total minus whatever you've already paid.

senses.head: Below zero on a scale
examples: It was minus twelve at the airport this morning.
The forecast has us at minus five by Sunday night.

senses.head: Commercial deduction
examples: Your share is the sale price minus closing costs.
The refund is the ticket price minus a $35 service fee.

senses.head: Informally, without — implying loss
examples: He came back from the trip minus a suitcase and a phone.
She showed up to the interview minus a résumé.

senses.head: Not a preposition — the adjective and the noun
body: No object follows either one.
examples: She got an A minus on the final. (adjective)
The commute is the one real minus of the job. (noun)

entries.русский: минус — вычитание и «ниже нуля»; разг. «без, лишившись» (came back minus a suitcase)
entries.register: neutral in arithmetic and commerce; informal in the "without" sense
entries.complement: noun phrase or a number — no gerund, no clause. The word is also an adjective (a minus sign, an A minus) and a noun (that's a real minus); in those uses it has no object and is not a preposition.
entries.pattern: [number] minus [number] · [amount] minus [deduction] · minus [number] degrees · [subject] [verb] minus [thing lost]
entries.contrast: Against less, which is the formal financial word for the same operation; against without, which is the neutral and unrestricted word for absence. Informal minus meaning "without" implies loss — you turn up minus something you should have had — which is why minus his jacket works and coffee minus sugar does not.
entries.see also: plus, less, give or take, without, free of, excluding, short of

entries.meaning: Corrects a total by naming what was left out of it. Nothing else in the exception family is so comfortable in speech while remaining perfectly precise.
examples: There were fourteen of us at dinner, not counting the kids.
She's read everything he wrote, not counting the early poems.
The drive takes about six hours, not counting stops.
It's a two-bedroom, not counting the office in the back.
We've spent around nine thousand, not counting what the permits cost.
He's been here twenty years, not counting the two he spent in Denver.

senses.head: Adjusting a head count
examples: There were fourteen of us at dinner, not counting the kids.
She's read everything he wrote, not counting the early poems.

senses.head: Adjusting a measurement or a duration
examples: The drive takes about six hours, not counting stops.
It's a two-bedroom, not counting the office in the back.

senses.head: Adjusting a sum or a span
examples: We've spent around nine thousand, not counting what the permits cost.
He's been here twenty years, not counting the two he spent in Denver.

entries.pronunciation note: the t of not goes to a glottal stop before the k, and the medial nt of counting drops · naht-KOWN-ting
entries.русский: не считая, без учёта — разговорная поправка к подсчёту
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, or gerund — never a finite clause. A what-phrase after it (not counting what the permits cost) is a fused relative, which is a noun phrase and not a clause; the test is that a plain noun can replace it (not counting the permit fees).
entries.pattern: [count or total], not counting [noun phrase] · [clause] not counting [verb-ing]
entries.variants: not including — interchangeable and a shade more formal
entries.contrast: The plain-speech version of excluding and exclusive of. It differs from except for in what it operates on: not counting the kids adjusts a number, while except for the kids qualifies a claim. Because it is transparently a negated participle, it can be used anywhere the arithmetic is being done out loud.
entries.see also: excluding, exclusive of, except for, including, minus

entries.meaning: Rules out everything but the named case, or says that a thing is of a different sort from what was expected. Its stock phrase other than that is one of the most common ways an American speaker signals that a report is otherwise complete.
examples: No one other than the account holder can request a copy.
The clinic accepts no payment other than cash.
We've never used the cabin other than in the summer.
Any use other than residential requires a variance.
He had no choice other than to take the plea.
There was nothing to do other than to wait it out.
She's fine, other than a bruised shoulder.
Other than that, the week was completely uneventful.

senses.head: Except, apart from
examples: No one other than the account holder can request a copy.
The clinic accepts no payment other than cash.

senses.head: Before an adjective, adverb, or prepositional phrase
examples: We've never used the cabin other than in the summer.
Any use other than residential requires a variance.

senses.head: Before a to-infinitive
examples: He had no choice other than to take the plea.
There was nothing to do other than to wait it out.

senses.head: The discourse formula
examples: She's fine, other than a bruised shoulder.
Other than that, the week was completely uneventful.

entries.русский: кроме, иной чем — подчёркивает инаковость; допускает и прилагательное, и наречие
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, adjective, adverb, prepositional phrase, gerund, or a to-infinitive (no choice other than to sue) — never a finite clause
entries.requires: usually a negative, a question, or a totalizing word nearby, much as but does — though it is freer than but and tolerates more.
entries.pattern: [negative or question] other than [noun phrase] · [clause], other than [adjective/adverb] · no choice other than to [verb] · Other than that, [clause]
entries.contrast: Other than and except for overlap heavily, but other than insists on difference of kind, which is what lets it take an adjective or an adverb where except for cannot: other than briefly, other than legal, other than in an emergency. Do not confuse it with rather than, which expresses a choice or a preference (walk rather than drive) and never an exception.
entries.see also: but, except for, besides, apart from, aside from

entries.meaning: Puts a case beyond the reach of the statement being made — either beyond a boundary, beyond a limit of competence, or beyond the scope of a general claim.
examples: Outside of a couple of late shifts, the schedule has been reasonable.
Nobody outside of the family knew he'd been sick.
Outside of Chicago, she's never lived in a big city.
That's outside of my area — you want the compliance desk.
Anything outside of routine maintenance needs written approval.
The pump is outside of warranty now.
They were standing outside of the courthouse when the verdict came down. (edit to outside the courthouse)
Park anywhere outside of the loading zone. (edit to outside the loading zone)
The dogs stayed outside all afternoon.
It's warm enough to eat outside tonight.

senses.head: Except for, apart from — chiefly American
examples: Outside of a couple of late shifts, the schedule has been reasonable.
Nobody outside of the family knew he'd been sick.
Outside of Chicago, she's never lived in a big city.

senses.head: Beyond the limits or the scope of
examples: That's outside of my area — you want the compliance desk.
Anything outside of routine maintenance needs written approval.
The pump is outside of warranty now.

senses.head: Spatially — where American editors cut the of
body: Correct in speech, but blue-penciled in edited prose.
examples: They were standing outside of the courthouse when the verdict came down. (edit to outside the courthouse)
Park anywhere outside of the loading zone. (edit to outside the loading zone)

senses.head: As an adverb — not a preposition
body: No of, no object.
examples: The dogs stayed outside all afternoon.
It's warm enough to eat outside tonight.

entries.pronunciation note: weak /ˌaʊtˈsaɪd əv/, reduced all the way to /ˌaʊtˈsaɪdə/ before a consonant — the of loses its /v/ exactly as it does in kind of and out of · owt-SYD uv
entries.русский: кроме, помимо (амер. разг.); а также «вне, за пределами» чьей-л. компетенции
entries.register: neutral to informal in the exception sense; chiefly American
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, or gerund — never a finite clause. Bare outside, with no of, is also an adverb that takes no object at all (she waited outside, let's eat outside); there it is not a preposition, and the test is exactly that — the preposition has an object, the adverb has none.
entries.pattern: Outside of [noun phrase], [clause] · [negative] outside of [noun phrase] · that's outside of [noun phrase] · [verb] outside (adverb — no object)
entries.variants: outside — the of is optional and usually dropped in the spatial sense (outside the courthouse), but obligatory in the exception sense: Outside a few typos is not idiomatic.
entries.contrast: The exception sense is an Americanism; British speakers avoid it and reach for apart from. In the spatial sense, American editors trim the of — outside the building, not outside of the building — and that spatial outside is covered with the position prepositions. Against apart from and aside from, outside of is the most conversational of the three.
entries.see also: apart from, aside from, besides, other than, short of

entries.meaning: Names the single survivor of a general negation. Almost every idiomatic use follows nothing, no one, all, or a description of emptiness, and the effect is elegiac in a way that except is not.
examples: All the crew were rescued save the engineer.
Nothing remained of the settlement save a chimney and a well.
He would tell them nothing save his name and the name of his ship.
The hall was dark save a single lamp at the far end.
Every window was shuttered save the one above the door.
There was nothing to do save wait for the tide to turn.
He could do nothing save watch the water come up over the sill.
The rights of the tenant are unaffected, save as provided in section 9.
All implied warranties are excluded, save as required by applicable law.
The two drafts are identical, save that the second one is dated. (conjunction — a clause follows)
He remembered nothing of the evening, save that it had rained. (conjunction)

senses.head: After a negative or a total
examples: All the crew were rescued save the engineer.
Nothing remained of the settlement save a chimney and a well.
He would tell them nothing save his name and the name of his ship.

senses.head: In descriptions of emptiness or silence
examples: The hall was dark save a single lamp at the far end.
Every window was shuttered save the one above the door.

senses.head: Before a bare infinitive
body: Only after a do-phrase, and never with to.
examples: There was nothing to do save wait for the tide to turn.
He could do nothing save watch the water come up over the sill.

senses.head: In legal drafting
body: The boilerplate save as otherwise provided is its last productive home.
examples: The rights of the tenant are unaffected, save as provided in section 9.
All implied warranties are excluded, save as required by applicable law.

senses.head: Not a preposition — the conjunction save that
body: The preposition takes an object; save that takes a whole finite clause with its own subject and verb.
examples: The two drafts are identical, save that the second one is dated. (conjunction — a clause follows)
He remembered nothing of the evening, save that it had rained. (conjunction)

entries.русский: книжн. кроме, за исключением — литературный и юридический двойник except
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, a prepositional phrase, or a bare infinitive after a do-phrase (nothing to do save wait); a finite clause only through save that, which is a conjunction. Never a gerund and never a to-infinitive.
entries.pattern: [negative or total] save [noun phrase] · save as provided in [clause reference] (legal) · nothing to do save [bare infinitive] · save that [clause] (conjunction)
entries.contrast: Save is except in a good suit. In American prose it reads as consciously literary, and it survives most naturally in legal drafting, where save as otherwise provided is standard boilerplate. Save for is the version most writers reach for now. Do not confuse the preposition with the verb save, from which it is historically distinct — this one came in from French sauf, "except".
entries.see also: save for, saving, except, but, bar

entries.meaning: Leaves one item behind after everything else has been cleared away. It is the descriptive writer's preposition, common in fiction and in longform journalism and almost absent from speech.
examples: The lobby was empty save for a security guard reading a paperback.
The field was bare save for a line of fence posts along the ridge.
He owned nothing save for the clothes he was wearing.
The record is spotless save for one late filing in 2009.
The town looks the same save for the boarded-up theater on Main.
She remembers nothing of the accident save for the smell of gasoline.
The trip went perfectly, save for having to change planes twice in one day.
The house came through the winter untouched, save for losing a few shingles off the back porch.

senses.head: Leaving one thing standing in an empty scene
body: The core use, and the reason writers prefer it to except for.
examples: The lobby was empty save for a security guard reading a paperback.
The field was bare save for a line of fence posts along the ridge.
He owned nothing save for the clothes he was wearing.

senses.head: Qualifying an otherwise clean record or an unchanged state
examples: The record is spotless save for one late filing in 2009.
The town looks the same save for the boarded-up theater on Main.
She remembers nothing of the accident save for the smell of gasoline.

senses.head: With a gerund
body: Possible but uncommon, and always a little stiff.
examples: The trip went perfectly, save for having to change planes twice in one day.
The house came through the winter untouched, save for losing a few shingles off the back porch.

entries.русский: книжн. кроме, если не считать — единственное, что уцелело в опустевшей картине
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun; a gerund is possible but uncommon. Never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [clause], save for [noun phrase] · Save for [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.contrast: The current literary equivalent of except for, and the form that has largely taken over from bare save. It carries a note of bareness or desolation that except for does not: writers use it when the exception is the only thing left standing in an otherwise empty scene.
entries.see also: save, except for, but for, saving

entries.meaning: Preserves one item from a sweeping provision. Where save subtracts a member from a set, saving protects a right or an interest from a rule that would otherwise reach it — which is exactly the job it still does in contracts.
examples: All previous agreements are terminated, saving the confidentiality provisions.
The judgment is affirmed, saving the appellant's right to seek further review.
The charter left the old privileges intact, saving the crown's right of appeal.
He spoke freely of the whole affair, saving the names of those involved.
Saving your presence, sir, the man is a fraud.
Saving your reverence, I never heard such nonsense in a courtroom.

senses.head: Preserving a right or a provision
examples: All previous agreements are terminated, saving the confidentiality provisions.
The judgment is affirmed, saving the appellant's right to seek further review.

senses.head: Preserving something from an older grant
examples: The charter left the old privileges intact, saving the crown's right of appeal.
He spoke freely of the whole affair, saving the names of those involved.

senses.head: The fixed apologetic formula
body: Saving your presence asks pardon for what the speaker is about to say. Wholly fossilized.
examples: Saving your presence, sir, the man is a fraud.
Saving your reverence, I never heard such nonsense in a courtroom.

entries.русский: устар./юр. за исключением, с сохранением — оговорка, защищающая право от общего правила
entries.complement: noun phrase — never a clause, never a gerund
entries.pattern: [clause], saving [noun phrase] · saving your presence (fixed formula)
entries.contrast: The participial twin of save, and the ancestor of the legal noun saving clause — the provision that preserves something the rest of a document would otherwise wipe out. Outside legal drafting and the fossilized apology saving your presence, no living American writes it; use excepting, excluding, or except for.
entries.see also: save, save for, excepting, bating

entries.meaning: Marks a point not reached — on a scale, on a road, or on a ladder of increasingly extreme measures. The third sense, where short is really the adjective and of the preposition, is the everyday one and shades into the others without a clean boundary.
examples: Donations stopped just short of the fundraising goal.
The car died a mile short of the exit.
Ticket sales came in a little short of two million.
Short of firing him, there isn't much the board can do.
Short of a miracle, that bridge won't reopen this year.
Nothing short of a subpoena will get those records released.
We're short of volunteers for Saturday.
The kitchen is two cooks short of what a Friday night needs.

senses.head: Not reaching a quantity, a distance, or a standard
examples: Donations stopped just short of the fundraising goal.
The car died a mile short of the exit.
Ticket sales came in a little short of two million.

senses.head: Except by resorting to
body: Naming the extreme measure that has been ruled out.
examples: Short of firing him, there isn't much the board can do.
Short of a miracle, that bridge won't reopen this year.
Nothing short of a subpoena will get those records released.

senses.head: Lacking, running low on
examples: We're short of volunteers for Saturday.
The kitchen is two cooks short of what a Friday night needs.

entries.pronunciation note: weak /ˈʃɔrt əv/, reduced /ˈʃɔrɾə/ with a flapped t and no /v/ at all — SHORT uv
entries.русский: не доходя до, не дотягивая до; «кроме как ценой» крайней меры; также «нуждаясь в»
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund — never a finite clause, never a to-infinitive
entries.pattern: [verb] short of [noun phrase] · Short of [verb-ing], [clause] · nothing short of [noun phrase] · be short of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Short of and barring both name a contingency, but short of names a drastic step you are declining to take, while barring names an accident you don't expect. Note also nothing short of and little short of, which are intensifiers rather than exceptions: nothing short of remarkable means "genuinely remarkable", not "except remarkable".
entries.see also: barring, failing, less, next to, minus

entries.respell: weak /tə ði ɪkˈskluʒən əv/, reduced /tə ði ɪkˈskluʒənə/
entries.meaning: Names what has been squeezed out by whatever the main clause is doing. It is a phrase of imbalance: outside a contract, nearly every use of it is a complaint that one activity has taken over the space that belonged to something else.
examples: He practiced to the exclusion of his schoolwork, his friends, and eventually his health.
The athletic department funds football to the exclusion of every other sport.
She read that winter to the exclusion of seeing anybody at all.
The team optimized for speed to the exclusion of testing anything properly.
For two years he worked on the manuscript to the exclusion of all else.
She talks about the lawsuit to the exclusion of everything else.
The court applied the plain language of the statute to the exclusion of the legislative history.
Hiring on test scores alone, to the exclusion of everything else a résumé shows, is how you end up with this staff.
The agreement grants the distributor the territory to the exclusion of all others.
The federal statute governs to the exclusion of any conflicting state rule.

senses.head: One pursuit crowding out everything else
body: The everyday use, and usually a criticism.
examples: He practiced to the exclusion of his schoolwork, his friends, and eventually his health.
The athletic department funds football to the exclusion of every other sport.

senses.head: With a gerund
examples: She read that winter to the exclusion of seeing anybody at all.
The team optimized for speed to the exclusion of testing anything properly.

senses.head: The fixed superlative tags
examples: For two years he worked on the manuscript to the exclusion of all else.
She talks about the lawsuit to the exclusion of everything else.

senses.head: Of a rule or a test that forces the alternatives out
examples: The court applied the plain language of the statute to the exclusion of the legislative history.
Hiring on test scores alone, to the exclusion of everything else a résumé shows, is how you end up with this staff.

senses.head: In law and contracts — exclusivity, with no criticism implied
examples: The agreement grants the distributor the territory to the exclusion of all others.
The federal statute governs to the exclusion of any conflicting state rule.

entries.русский: в ущерб всему остальному — не изъятие из множества, а вытеснение прочего
entries.register: formal to neutral; at home in criticism, in psychology, and in contracts
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, possessive plus noun, or gerund (to the exclusion of sleeping) — never a finite clause and never a to-infinitive: ✗ to the exclusion of to sleep. The to is a preposition, so the -ing is obligatory, exactly as it is after in addition to.
entries.pattern: [verb phrase] to the exclusion of [noun phrase] · [verb phrase] to the exclusion of [verb-ing] · to the exclusion of all else
entries.variants: to the exclusion of all else and to the exclusion of everything else — the two fixed superlative tags, and the commonest shapes the phrase takes outside a contract.
entries.contrast: The one entry in this section that is not an exception word. Excluding, except for, and with the exception of take a member out of a set; to the exclusion of names what got crowded out because something else took up all the room. She studies history excluding the war years subtracts a period from her subject; she studies the war years to the exclusion of everything else says the war years have eaten her whole subject. It therefore attaches to a verb phrase rather than to a noun, and unlike the rest of this family it cannot open a sentence: ✗ To the exclusion of her friends, she trained. Against instead of, which names a straight substitution and implies no excess; against at the expense of, its closest neighbor, which stresses the price paid rather than the crowding out. In legal drafting it has a fourth, unemotional use — a grant to the exclusion of all others is a grant of exclusivity, with no criticism implied at all.
entries.see also: excluding, exclusive of, with the exception of, including without limitation, short of, instead of

entries.respell: weak /wəθ ði ɪkˈsɛpʃən əv/, reduced /wəθ ði ɪkˈsɛpʃənə/
entries.meaning: Lifts one named item out of an otherwise universal statement, slowly and on the record. The claim it modifies has to be a genuine generalization — subtracting from a statement about a single thing produces nonsense.
examples: Every state with the exception of Nebraska has a two-chamber legislature.
With the exception of Tuesday, the entire week is booked.
The building came through the storm undamaged, with the exception of two broken windows.
All fees are refundable, with the exception of the application charge.
With the sole exception of the treasurer, no one on the board had seen the numbers.
With the possible exception of 1998, this is the wettest spring on record.
The trip went smoothly, with the exception of having to change planes in Dallas.
The renovation stayed on budget, with the exception of having to replace the wiring on the second floor.

senses.head: Subtracting one member from a universal claim
examples: Every state with the exception of Nebraska has a two-chamber legislature.
With the exception of Tuesday, the entire week is booked.

senses.head: In reports, findings, and inventories
examples: The building came through the storm undamaged, with the exception of two broken windows.
All fees are refundable, with the exception of the application charge.

senses.head: The emphatic and hedged expansions
examples: With the sole exception of the treasurer, no one on the board had seen the numbers.
With the possible exception of 1998, this is the wettest spring on record.

senses.head: With a gerund
body: Grammatical, but heavy enough that except for is usually better.
examples: The trip went smoothly, with the exception of having to change planes in Dallas.
The renovation stayed on budget, with the exception of having to replace the wiring on the second floor.

entries.русский: за исключением — офиц. развёрнутое except for; выделяет один пункт из общего правила
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun; a gerund is possible but uncommon (with the exception of having to change planes). Never a finite clause — for a clause, write except that.
entries.pattern: With the exception of [noun phrase], [clause] · [clause], with the exception of [noun phrase] · [subject], with the exception of [noun phrase], [verb agreeing with the subject]
entries.variants: with the sole exception of (emphatic), with the possible exception of (hedging) — the two standard expansions, and the reason the long form survives at all
entries.contrast: The longest word for the shortest job. Except for, apart from, aside from, other than, and bare except all subtract the same item in a third of the space, and in ordinary prose one of them is the better choice. Reach for the long form when the exception must be foregrounded, when a document has to be unmistakable about which element the exception attaches to, or when with the possible exception of is doing real hedging that no shorter phrase can do. Like everything else in this file it is a preposition, so it leaves the number of the verb alone: Every state, with the exception of Nebraska, has two chambers.
entries.see also: except for, except, apart from, other than, save for, excepting, leaving aside

entries.meaning: Declares a required thing to be missing and states what follows from its absence. It is one of the few prepositions that entered general American usage straight out of judicial opinions, and it still carries their tone.
examples: Absent a written waiver, the filing deadline stands.
Absent an emergency, visits are limited to two hours.
Absent some showing of prejudice, the court will not disturb the verdict.
Absent any objection from the neighbors, the variance will be granted.
Absent new funding, the program shuts down in June.
Absent clear direction from the board, the staff did what seemed reasonable.

senses.head: Naming a missing document or authorization
examples: Absent a written waiver, the filing deadline stands.
Absent an emergency, visits are limited to two hours.

senses.head: Naming a missing showing or proof
examples: Absent some showing of prejudice, the court will not disturb the verdict.
Absent any objection from the neighbors, the variance will be granted.

senses.head: Naming a missing condition in policy or business writing
examples: Absent new funding, the program shuts down in June.
Absent clear direction from the board, the staff did what seemed reasonable.

entries.pronunciation note: first-syllable stress, unlike the verb absent /æbˈsɛnt/ (he absented himself)
entries.русский: юр., амер. при отсутствии, за неимением — называет недостающее условие (absent proof)
entries.complement: noun phrase, usually indefinite — a gerund is possible but rare even in legal writing, and a finite clause is impossible: write absent evidence that…, or switch to unless
entries.pattern: Absent [noun phrase], [clause] · [clause] absent [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The legal register's without or in the absence of. Against barring, which names an intervening event, absent names a missing prerequisite; against but for, which looks back at a counterfactual, absent looks forward to a condition that has not been met. British editors still flag it as an Americanism; American courts and regulators use it constantly.
entries.see also: without, in the absence of, failing, barring, but for, if not for, sans

entries.respell: weak /ˈfri əv/, reduced /ˈfriə/ before a consonant
entries.meaning: Reports that an unwelcome thing is missing and counts that as good news. It is the positive face of the absence family and the only member with approval built into it.
examples: Delivery within the county is free of charge.
The account is free of monthly maintenance fees.
The lot is free of debris and ready for the foundation.
The samples came back free of any sign of contamination.
The title is free of liens and easements.
They retired free of debt for the first time in thirty years.
For one summer she was free of having to answer to anybody.
The new job leaves him free of commuting three hours a day.

senses.head: Free of a cost or a charge
examples: Delivery within the county is free of charge.
The account is free of monthly maintenance fees.

senses.head: Free of a contaminant or a defect
examples: The lot is free of debris and ready for the foundation.
The samples came back free of any sign of contamination.

senses.head: Free of an obligation or an encumbrance
examples: The title is free of liens and easements.
They retired free of debt for the first time in thirty years.

senses.head: With a gerund
examples: For one summer she was free of having to answer to anybody.
The new job leaves him free of commuting three hours a day.

entries.pronunciation note: the of loses its /v/ as it does in kind of · FREE uv
entries.русский: свободный от, без — об отсутствии нежелательного, как о благе: free of charge «бесплатно»
entries.complement: noun phrase, usually with no determiner (free of charge, free of debt, free of liens), or a gerund (free of having to report to anyone) — never a finite clause and never a to-infinitive: ✗ free of to pay.
entries.pattern: [noun] free of [noun phrase] · [subject] is free of [noun phrase] · free of [verb-ing]
entries.variants: free from — the two overlap, but free of prefers a physical or financial contaminant (free of dust, free of debt) and free from prefers an oppression or a constraint (free from fear, free from interference). Devoid of is the cold formal version and is always a criticism.
entries.contrast: Against without, which merely reports that a thing is missing, free of reports the absence as a benefit — whatever is missing is something you would not have wanted. That is why free of charge is idiomatic and ✗ free of a roof is not, and it is the one respect in which this preposition is not interchangeable with without, sans, or minus. Against exclusive of, which is bookkeeping for what a figure leaves out rather than a claim about anybody's good fortune.
entries.see also: without, sans, absent, in the absence of, exclusive of, minus

entries.respell: weak /ɪn ði ˈæbsəns əv/, reduced /ɪn ði ˈæbsənsə/
entries.meaning: States the negative condition under which the main clause holds. It is the standard opening of a default rule: this is what happens when the thing that ought to be there isn't.
examples: In the absence of a written agreement, state law governs.
In the absence of any objection, the motion carries.
In the absence of evidence, the committee declined to act.
In the absence of a diagnosis, the insurer refused to pay the claim.
Plants grown in the absence of light lose their color within days.
In the absence of oxygen, the reaction stops cold.

senses.head: Naming a missing document, rule, or authority
examples: In the absence of a written agreement, state law governs.
In the absence of any objection, the motion carries.

senses.head: Naming missing evidence or information
examples: In the absence of evidence, the committee declined to act.
In the absence of a diagnosis, the insurer refused to pay the claim.

senses.head: In scientific and technical description
body: Here the absence is a controlled condition, not a failure.
examples: Plants grown in the absence of light lose their color within days.
In the absence of oxygen, the reaction stops cold.

entries.русский: офиц. при отсутствии, за неимением — условие, при котором действует правило по умолчанию
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective-case pronoun, usually indefinite or non-count. No gerund, and never a finite clause: write in the absence of any evidence that…, or switch to the conjunction unless.
entries.pattern: In the absence of [noun phrase], [clause] · [clause] in the absence of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The unfolded, fully explicit without, and the drafting register's absent. Three registers of one idea: without a permit is what a person says, absent a permit is what a court writes, in the absence of a permit is what a regulation writes. Against failing, which frames the missing thing as a prerequisite somebody was supposed to supply, in the absence of is neutral about fault. Keep the frozen preposition apart from the live phrase in The vice chair presides in the absence of the chair, where absence still means somebody is away — the same five words doing an entirely different job.
entries.see also: without, absent, failing, but for, sans

entries.respell: weak /ˈnɛks tə/ (the medial t usually drops)
entries.meaning: Squeezes a quantity or a quality down to the edge of zero. The ranking sense — "second only to" — is the same geometry applied to a list rather than to a scale.
examples: The car sold for next to nothing at the county auction.
He knows next to nothing about wiring.
There's next to no parking on that block after five.
Getting a permit downtown is next to impossible.
The insulation in this place is next to useless.
Next to her sister, she's the fastest swimmer on the team.
Next to sleeping, reading is his favorite way to kill an afternoon.

senses.head: Almost nothing, hardly any
examples: The car sold for next to nothing at the county auction.
He knows next to nothing about wiring.
There's next to no parking on that block after five.

senses.head: Practically, all but — before an adjective
examples: Getting a permit downtown is next to impossible.
The insulation in this place is next to useless.

senses.head: Second only to — ranking
examples: Next to her sister, she's the fastest swimmer on the team.
Next to sleeping, reading is his favorite way to kill an afternoon.

entries.русский: почти, практически (next to nothing «почти ничего»); а также «уступая только кому-л.»
entries.complement: in the limiting sense, only nothing, no + noun, or an adjective — not an ordinary noun phrase. Next to nothing means "hardly anything"; next to money means nothing at all. In the ranking sense ("second only to") it does take an ordinary noun phrase or a gerund — next to her sister, next to sleeping. Never a finite clause in either sense. The spatial next to, which takes any noun phrase, is covered with the position prepositions.
entries.pattern: next to nothing · next to no [noun] · next to [adjective] · Next to [noun phrase], [superlative claim] (ranking)
entries.contrast: In the limiting sense it is a near-synonym of all but (all but impossible) and little short of, and it cannot be swapped for the spatial next to without changing the word class of what follows: next to the bank is a place, next to nothing is a quantity. British and American usage agree completely here.
entries.see also: short of, but, minus, without

entries.meaning: Reports absence with an arched eyebrow. Americans meet it most often in Shakespeare's catalogue of old age and in the type specimen book, and use it themselves mainly for effect.
examples: He took the meeting sans tie, which for him counted as rebellion.
A martini sans olive is just cold gin.
The remake is the original sans charm.
She showed up to the gala sans jewelry, sans makeup, sans apology.
Jaques ends his speech "sans teeth, sans eyes, sans taste, sans everything."
It's a Western sans horses, which is either brave or a mistake.
A weeknight lasagna sans the four-hour sauce. (the determiner here is a copywriter's liberty)

senses.head: Plain absence, delivered as a wink
body: Always a bare noun, never sans the.
examples: He took the meeting sans tie, which for him counted as rebellion.
A martini sans olive is just cold gin.
The remake is the original sans charm.

senses.head: The rhetorical series
body: Repeated for cumulative effect — the construction Shakespeare fixed in the language.
examples: She showed up to the gala sans jewelry, sans makeup, sans apology.
Jaques ends his speech "sans teeth, sans eyes, sans taste, sans everything."

senses.head: In headline, menu, and catalog copy
body: Where brevity rather than wit is the motive.
examples: It's a Western sans horses, which is either brave or a mistake.
A weeknight lasagna sans the four-hour sauce. (the determiner here is a copywriter's liberty)

entries.pronunciation note: anglicized; the French /sɑ̃/ only when the speaker is being deliberately French
entries.русский: книжн./шутл. без — нарочитый вариант without; всегда с голым существительным, без артикля
entries.complement: a bare noun phrase, usually with no determiner — sans makeup, not sans the makeup. Never a finite clause, and a gerund only as a joke.
entries.pattern: [clause] sans [bare noun] · sans [noun], sans [noun], sans [noun] (the rhetorical series)
entries.contrast: A self-conscious without. Borrowed from French in the fourteenth century, dropped, and revived as a mannerism, it now signals wit or style rather than plain absence. Note that sans serif is a frozen typographic compound, not a live preposition. Where without is invisible, sans is always noticed — which is the only reason to use it.
entries.see also: without, minus, absent, short of

entries.meaning: The most heavily used preposition in this file and the most versatile. Its range runs from a missing spoonful of sugar to a counterfactual that reorganizes the whole sentence, and its gerund construction — without saying goodbye — is the standard English way of saying "and did not".
examples: She drinks her coffee without sugar.
A house without a roof isn't worth much.
He walked out without his keys.
They went to the game without me.
He left without saying goodbye to anyone.
You can't cancel without giving thirty days' notice.
The bill passed without a single senator reading it.
We finished the job without anyone getting hurt.
Without your help, we'd still be arguing about the budget.
Without the levee, half the town would have flooded.
There's no coffee left, so we'll have to do without.
They went without for most of that winter.
The old road still runs without the city gates.
"There is a green hill far away, without a city wall."

senses.head: Not having, lacking
examples: She drinks her coffee without sugar.
A house without a roof isn't worth much.

senses.head: Not accompanied by
examples: He walked out without his keys.
They went to the game without me.

senses.head: Followed by a gerund — "and not doing the thing named"
examples: He left without saying goodbye to anyone.
You can't cancel without giving thirty days' notice.

senses.head: Followed by an object and a gerund
examples: The bill passed without a single senator reading it.
We finished the job without anyone getting hurt.

senses.head: Counterfactually — "if there were not" or "if there had not been"
examples: Without your help, we'd still be arguing about the budget.
Without the levee, half the town would have flooded.

senses.head: As an adverb, with no object
body: After do, go, and manage.
examples: There's no coffee left, so we'll have to do without.
They went without for most of that winter.

senses.head: Archaically, "outside"
body: The original sense, now confined to older writing and hymn texts. This is the with + out the word was built from.
examples: The old road still runs without the city gates.
"There is a green hill far away, without a city wall."

entries.русский: без — отсутствие; с герундием «не делая чего-л.»; а также «если бы не» в сослагательном
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective-case pronoun, gerund, or object + gerund (without anyone noticing). It can also stand alone as an adverb with no object after do, go, and manage (we'll have to do without). It can never take a finite clause and never a to-infinitive: not without to pay, not without he agrees.
entries.pattern: without [noun phrase] · without [verb-ing] · without [noun phrase] [verb-ing] · do / go / manage without (no object)
entries.contrast: The negative counterpart of with, and the center the whole absence family orbits: sans is its literary pose, minus its informal one, absent its legal one, in the absence of its bureaucratic one, and free of the one that treats the missing thing as good riddance. Against but for, without covers both plain absence (coffee without sugar) and counterfactual absence (without you, I'd have quit), where but for can only do the second. The regional conjunction without meaning "unless" (I won't go without you come along) is nonstandard in written American English.
entries.see also: with, sans, absent, in the absence of, free of, minus, but for, if not for, failing
